The European Union (EU) faces a number of pressing challenges. It must enhance the competitiveness of its existing industries and invest in the technologies of the future, strengthen its defence capabilities, agree on its long-term budget, forge new partnerships and step up efforts to combat climate change. Germany has a pivotal role to play in addressing these challenges. The Federal Government has declared its ambition to take on a leading role within the EU. But how do German citizens perceive their country’s role in the Union? What do they consider to be the key priorities? This study seeks to foster an empirically grounded debate on the future of Germany’s European policy. Drawing on eight years of survey data, it provides a frame of reference for the strategic direction of that policy, offering context and guidance for its development.

Key Findings of the Representative Survey1

Benefits of EU membership outweigh drawbacks; crises best addressed at EU level: The majority of respondents remain positive about Germany’s membership in the EU. For 63 per cent, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks. Most respondents believe that current crises are more likely to be resolved at EU (54 per cent) than at national level (38 per cent). This preference extends across all surveyed policy areas (only exception: economy, 35 per cent): climate/environmental protection (65 per cent), defence (63 per cent), foreign policy (59 per cent), migration/asylum (57 per cent), digitalisation/AI (52 per cent). 

Call for proactive approach; majority supports compromises and pioneer coalitions: 68 per cent of respondents believe that the German Government should play an active role within the EU. Also, 59 per cent support joint decision-making to ensure a strong Europe, even if this requires Germany to make compromises. In addition, 72 per cent favour the option of ‘pioneer coalitions’ when vetoes lead to deadlock. 

Shifting priorities for additional EU investment: less emphasis on defence, greater support for climate action and social protection: Although respondents remain sceptical about the level of Germany’s contribution to the EU budget, they support increased joint spending in specific policy areas, particularly internal security (41 per cent). Support for additional defence spending has fallen from 52 per cent in 2025 to 31 per cent. By contrast, support for spending on social security has risen from 23 per cent to 39 per cent, and on climate and environmental protection from 25 per cent to 37 per cent.

Majority oppose relaxing climate targets: A combined majority of 62 per cent want the German Government to advocate in Brussels for maintaining the EU’s existing climate targets (36 per cent) or setting even more ambitious targets (26 per cent). By contrast, 33 per cent favour relaxing the EU’s climate targets.

Strong support for measures to strengthen European industry, despite the costs: There is strong support for industrial and trade policy measures aimed at strengthening the European economy and enhancing its resilience. 88 per cent of respondents support onshoring, even if it entails higher costs; 77 per cent back a ‘buy European’ approach; and 65 per cent support tariffs on low-cost imports from China.

Calls for greater independence from the US; split priorities regarding basis for new partnerships and EU enlargement: According to 76 per cent of respondents, Europe should become more independent of the US and seek new partnerships. 49 per cent believe such partnerships should strengthen joint values (democracy, human rights), while 47 per cent prioritise economic and security interests. Support for EU enlargement is more limited: 40 per cent of respondents are in favour, while 49 per cent oppose it.

Trends and Policy Recommendations

Build European sovereignty through cooperation: The call for European sovereignty is a recurring theme throughout the findings, encompassing the EU’s capacity to act, industrial resilience and independence from the US. Germany’s European policy should seek to build a cooperative European sovereignty, not by pursuing isolationism, but by forging diversified partnerships guided by shared values and interests. 

Deepen EU Single Market; strengthen EU industry: The German Government should pursue an EU economic policy that deepens the Single Market by removing internal trade barriers and advancing the Capital Markets Union, while strengthening EU industry through joint investment and industrial policy instruments. This would help demonstrate the EU’s capacity to address economic challenges.

Integrate Europe’s defence industry; avoid excessive costs and monopolies: Rather than focusing on national targets and market share, Germany should pursue a clear European approach to defence, prioritising cost-effectiveness and interoperability while preventing dependencies, monopolies and windfall profits. 

Maintain climate ambitions; strengthen EU’s social dimension: A clear majority favour increased joint spending on social protection, climate and environmental protection, and support the EU’s climate targets. Germany’s European policy should therefore strengthen the EU’s social dimension and actively defend its climate targets. 

Focus the EU budget on EU added value: Rather than focusing on Germany’s net contribution to the EU budget, the German Government should highlight the benefits of joint investment, explain the need to fund solutions at EU level and ensure that funds are spent efficiently, with a clear focus on EU added value.

The summary of the study is available as a PDF here.

1 For this study, pollytix strategic research GmbH conducted an online survey of 3,023 people on behalf of the Heinrich Böll Foundation between 27 August and 4 September 2026. The results are representative of voting-eligible citizens aged 18 and over. The margin of statistical error for the overall results ranges from ±1.1 to ±1.8 percentage points.

There is also broad support for a stronger European economy, even if this comes at a higher cost. These are among the findings of this year’s edition of our study on Germany’s role in the EU. Dr. Maria Skóra, Georg McCutcheon

November 21, 2025, 5 p.m. As on every Friday, a long line of women sits on the ground along the ochre-colored walls of Figuig City Hall. Wrapped in the white of their haïks, woolen robes, these women have been the driving force behind a citizens’ resistance movement for two years: the Hirak al-Ma‘, Arabic for “water movement.” “The water of Figuig is not for sale,” they chant. And: “No to the company!” Amid the sea of white, 66-year-old Fatima carries memories of an oasis that the new generation knows only from the stories of their elders. Her eyes light up when she talks about her youth in the heart of the palm grove: “My childhood memories are inextricably linked to our gardens. There were wonderful pools and canals where we used to swim. Our childhood was marked by abundance and the sound of water.”

Figuig lies at an elevation of 900 meters in the far southeast of Morocco. It consists of seven villages spread over an area of 35 km² and has just over 10,000 residents. Figuig is a green island surrounded by mountains and bordered on three sides by Algeria. For centuries, people here have lived in an isolated world. They rely solely on themselves and the groundwater. 

“Our water has always belonged to us,” says Naïma, a farmer who took over the family farm. “It was our ancestors who built the khettaras [underground irrigation systems]. If a company comes and takes our resource away, the oasis will disappear. We won’t let that happen. We’re fighting for future generations.”

The company the farmer is referring to is a government project. In 2023, the government passed Law 83-21, which provides for the establishment of regional companies (Sociétés Régionales Multi-services / SRM) to manage water, electricity, and wastewater. In Figuig, this decision was perceived as an attempt to strip the oasis of its identity. Here, water is not a commodity that can be managed by a company 400 kilometers away; it is the blood that flows through the veins of the palm grove, a common good made available by the hard work of the ancestors.

Water as Heritage

“The oasis is not a product of nature,” explains Majid Boudia. In 2022, the farmer and expert played a key role in getting Figuig’s recognized by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) as part of the Global Agricultural Heritage System (SIPAM). “Our ancestors made use of sophisticated irrigation systems, groundwater, and the cultivation of palm trees and other species to transform this part of the desert into a habitat. This traditional knowledge, based on water management and solidarity, is crucial to our survival and our culture.” Historically, the oasis was far more than just an agricultural area: it was the economic heart of the desert, an indispensable hub for caravans, and a stop for pilgrims on their way to the holy sites.

The secret to Figuig’s survival cannot be seen; you have to hear it. Here, water gushes from 17 artesian wells with temperatures ranging from 31 °C to 37 °C. 

Majid points out the Agoudass, a stone structure housing a water distribution system. The inhabitants of Figuig built it centuries ago. It looks like a clockwork made of stone, with bright blue-painted channels tracing a geometric pattern on the floor. In the Agoudass, Majid acts like a conductor. With the precision of a watchmaker, he manipulates the pebbles and cloths used to direct the flow of water. To gain more freedom, the Figuiguis have built about 200 storage basins. These reservoirs serve as regulators: they collect water at night to enable irrigation during the day. This way, water is available on demand. This system saves a lot of work: in the past, women had to carry 30-liter clay pots for miles to supply their families with water. 

The drinking water network is the result of a collective pledge, a collaborative and communal effort

With the founding of the agricultural community in 1963, public wells were installed near the homes. Subsequently, a joint agreement between the community and the oasis residents enabled the construction of a drinking water network. This network was neither financed nor built by the central government. It is the result of a collective pledge, a collaborative and communal effort known as Twiza: each family “sacrificed” a portion of their private water rights for the common good, and each contributed according to their means to dig the ground, purchase the materials, and install the first faucets. By building their own infrastructure, the Figuigis established an inalienable right known as Haq l-ma, the right to water. To ensure the maintenance of the pipelines, the residents agreed to pay a symbolic fee to the municipality, which has committed to providing the oasis with roads, electricity, and infrastructure.

These efforts explain why, until today, the residents believe that the water belongs to them and not to the state. “In the oasis, we were raised to believe that water is precious, that you don’t waste anything, and that you reuse every drop. Over the centuries, this understanding of the resource has evolved into a culture of survival and created a social cohesion that persists to this day,” says Majid Boudia. Even the transition to a municipal city administration in 1994 did not end the social contract. Today, it forms the strongest bulwark against the reform. For Majid and his family, the principle is clear: what has been built communally cannot be privatized.

The Art of Scarcity

The conflict that divides Figuig today centers on a single piece of legislation: Law 83-21. For the authorities, the creation of regional water management companies (SRMs) represents an inevitable modernization of resource management. In the face of growing water scarcity, it is intended to prevent water from being wasted. For the people of Figuig, this represents a brutal break with a system of collective management that has always been regarded as an non-negotiable common good.

This bond has nothing sentimental about it, says Samira Mizbar, a social economist from Figuig. It is contractually regulated and legally unambiguous. 

“The springs that supply Figuig belong to families. This right is enshrined in the official gazette,” the social scientist points out. “Every beneficiary is listed there with their exact share.” 

Fatiha Kadi of the Water Movement believes that this resource comes with a duty to be vigilant: “The fact that we still have water today is no coincidence; it’s because we’ve mastered the art of scarcity. We live in harmony with the rhythm of the water. When it is abundant, we use it; when it becomes scarce, we conserve it.” She points out that the water travels phenomenal distances from the Atlas Mountains to reach this land, where the sky provides only 120 millimeters of rain per year. “Every drop that arrives here is a miracle that has crossed the mountains.“

Even though the SRM is presented as a national project to secure the water supply, doubts remain in the oasis. “We’ve known for centuries how to deal with water scarcity. If the government really wants to secure the water supply, why does it continue to allow the construction of wells and motor pumps?” asks Majid Bouida.

The entire natural balance of the oasis microclimate is at risk of collapsing.

Figuig sits atop an aquifer whose centuries-old balance is now threatened by the combined effects of climate change and overuse. In 2021, a report by the FAO revealed an alarming reality: within fifty years, seventeen of the oasis’s thirty-nine historic springs have dried up. The total available water supply has shrunk significantly—from 300 to 180 liters per second. According to Majid Boudia, this decline is not an inevitable consequence of climate change. “Certainly, climate change and drought play a role, but it is primarily human pressure that is destroying the oasis.”

The Struggle for Control

In 2010, construction began on the Sfissef Dam, 30 kilometers northwest of Figuig, which went into operation in 2015. By creating an illusion of security, it encouraged investment in palm varieties such as Mejhoul, which consume extremely large amounts of water. As soon as the drought had drained the dam, landowners turned en masse to groundwater. In 2021 alone, 1,338 wells were dug.

As the water level drops, an invisible enemy rises from the depths: salt, which could make the oasis gardens infertile for good. “With the loss of control over water, the entire natural balance of the oasis microclimate is at risk of collapsing,” says Boudia.

In fact, the palm groves in many of Morocco’s oases have been transformed into highly simplified agricultural systems as part of a trend of modernization. 

While these may be potentially more productive, they are also more vulnerable to water scarcity.

To appease the Hirak movement, the authorities organized several meetings with its members. They explained that the SRM is a state-owned enterprise that plans neither to privatize nor to increase the prices. But the wording of the law speaks a different language. For example, Article 2 provides for the establishment of a public limited company (SA) under commercial law with an industrial purpose. It is intended to manage water resources in the future. Article 3 specifies that the capital may be opened to the private sector, provided that the state’s stake does not fall below ten percent. 

“An SA is a business,” says Samira Mizbar, arguing that the government wants to turn water into a commodity that is billed. “That’s unacceptable, especially since a large portion of the population can’t afford it.” Faced with this impasse, the protesters have turned to the Kingdom’s Ombudsman’s Office. Even though no tangible results have been achieved so far, giving up is not an option. “Giving up would mean leaving Figuig. And that’s out of the question,” Samira emphasizes.

One Million Minutes of Resistance

The Hirak in Figuig started small. In October 2023, two days before the first vote on the implementation of Law 83-21 in the municipal council, six people demonstrated in front of City Hall. A young photographer live-streamed the sit-in on Facebook. Ultimately, the municipal council voted for joining the controversial SRM by a very narrow majority. Soon after, a sense of having been betrayed by politicians led to the creation of the local coordinating body for advocacy on matters concerning the Figuig oasis.

One of the water movement’s greatest achievements was breaking through Figuig’s geographical isolation by building national support alliances.

A coalition now includes 24 members, among them labor unions, human rights organizations, and feminist movements. 

These supporters gathered at the oasis as part of a solidarity caravan that traveled from Casablanca through several cities to Figuig. They made it clear that Figuig’s problem is not a local dispute, but a matter of sovereignty and human rights. 

Meanwhile, the water movement is making its voice heard at the national level: through a study meeting in the heart of parliament or at major national and international conferences on water scarcity and climate change. On September 26, 2025, the movement reached a staggering milestone: one million minutes of resistance—through sit-ins under the scorching sun or in the bitter cold of the mountains, through nighttime marches by the light of cell phone flashlights, or concerts with cooking pots.

Women are the true driving force: they are resilient, deeply rooted, and ready to do whatever it takes to protect our water.

Women have always been at the forefront of this movement, wearing their traditional white robes. The haïk, which was once reserved for the elderly or for work in the fields, has become a powerful symbol for political communication. The garment serves as a reminder of past struggles, says Fatiha Kadi: “It is an echo of the resistance against colonialism and during the years of the ‘Lead Era.’” The women of Figuig have always been resistance fighters and a role model for all of Morocco, she adds. “By wearing the haïk, they protect their dignity in the face of what they call the new neoliberal colonialism.”

Water in Morocco

  • Morocco is at risk of losing 80 percent of its water resources within the next 25 years.
  • The fill rate of Moroccan reservoirs fell from 61.1 percent to 29.1 percent between 2018 and 2023.
  • 50 percent of Morocco's rainfall is concentrated in just 7 percent of the country's land area, which means that more than 90 percent of the country receives only 50 percent of the rainfall.
  • Morocco plans to make massive investments in desalination – 20 plants are set to be built by 2030.

The role of women in the Figuig Hirak goes beyond their mere numerical presence; they are the true driving force. “I have always compared the women of Figuig to our palm trees,” says Zoubida Benali, a member of the Water Hirak coordination group. “The palm tree is incredibly resilient: it consumes only what is necessary to survive, yet is capable of spreading its roots over incredible distances to absorb even the slightest trace of moisture. The women here are just the same. They are resilient, deeply rooted, and ready to do whatever it takes to protect our water.”

The central role of women can also be explained by a demographic reality. As economic pressure drives men to migrate to the cities, women have become the pillars of the oasis economy—whether through agricultural work or business operations. Fatima Kandar, 63, embodies their perseverance. At the head of a wool cooperative and an association for the protection of cultural heritage, she uses poetry as a lever of resistance. “I’ve never seen the inside of a school, but the words know where to find me. The poems come to me all on their own. Thanks to the Hirak, my voice has been heard everywhere, and it won’t be silenced.”

 A detailed version of the text in French is available on the website of the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s Morocco office.
items.title: Guardians of the Blue Gold Scrollytelling In Morocco, far from the capital Rabat, women in a desert oasis are defying a law that seeks to abolish their centuries-old right to the communal management of water distribution – through sit-in strikes, marches and, to date, one million minutes of resistance. Dounia Z. Mseffer, Hannah El-Hitami

November 21, 2025, 5 p.m. As on every Friday, a long line of women sits on the ground along the ochre-colored walls of Figuig City Hall. Wrapped in the white of their haïks, woolen robes, these women have been the driving force behind a citizens’ resistance movement for two years: the Hirak al-Ma‘, Arabic for “water movement.” “The water of Figuig is not for sale,” they chant. And: “No to the company!” Amid the sea of white, 66-year-old Fatima carries memories of an oasis that the new generation knows only from the stories of their elders. Her eyes light up when she talks about her youth in the heart of the palm grove: “My childhood memories are inextricably linked to our gardens. There were wonderful pools and canals where we used to swim. Our childhood was marked by abundance and the sound of water.”

Figuig lies at an elevation of 900 meters in the far southeast of Morocco. It consists of seven villages spread over an area of 35 km² and has just over 10,000 residents. Figuig is a green island surrounded by mountains and bordered on three sides by Algeria. For centuries, people here have lived in an isolated world. They rely solely on themselves and the groundwater. 

“Our water has always belonged to us,” says Naïma, a farmer who took over the family farm. “It was our ancestors who built the khettaras [underground irrigation systems]. If a company comes and takes our resource away, the oasis will disappear. We won’t let that happen. We’re fighting for future generations.”

The company the farmer is referring to is a government project. In 2023, the government passed Law 83-21, which provides for the establishment of regional companies (Sociétés Régionales Multi-services / SRM) to manage water, electricity, and wastewater. In Figuig, this decision was perceived as an attempt to strip the oasis of its identity. Here, water is not a commodity that can be managed by a company 400 kilometers away; it is the blood that flows through the veins of the palm grove, a common good made available by the hard work of the ancestors.

Water as Heritage

“The oasis is not a product of nature,” explains Majid Boudia. In 2022, the farmer and expert played a key role in getting Figuig’s recognized by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) as part of the Global Agricultural Heritage System (SIPAM). “Our ancestors made use of sophisticated irrigation systems, groundwater, and the cultivation of palm trees and other species to transform this part of the desert into a habitat. This traditional knowledge, based on water management and solidarity, is crucial to our survival and our culture.” Historically, the oasis was far more than just an agricultural area: it was the economic heart of the desert, an indispensable hub for caravans, and a stop for pilgrims on their way to the holy sites.

The secret to Figuig’s survival cannot be seen; you have to hear it. Here, water gushes from 17 artesian wells with temperatures ranging from 31 °C to 37 °C. 

Majid points out the Agoudass, a stone structure housing a water distribution system. The inhabitants of Figuig built it centuries ago. It looks like a clockwork made of stone, with bright blue-painted channels tracing a geometric pattern on the floor. In the Agoudass, Majid acts like a conductor. With the precision of a watchmaker, he manipulates the pebbles and cloths used to direct the flow of water. To gain more freedom, the Figuiguis have built about 200 storage basins. These reservoirs serve as regulators: they collect water at night to enable irrigation during the day. This way, water is available on demand. This system saves a lot of work: in the past, women had to carry 30-liter clay pots for miles to supply their families with water. 

The drinking water network is the result of a collective pledge, a collaborative and communal effort

With the founding of the agricultural community in 1963, public wells were installed near the homes. Subsequently, a joint agreement between the community and the oasis residents enabled the construction of a drinking water network. This network was neither financed nor built by the central government. It is the result of a collective pledge, a collaborative and communal effort known as Twiza: each family “sacrificed” a portion of their private water rights for the common good, and each contributed according to their means to dig the ground, purchase the materials, and install the first faucets. By building their own infrastructure, the Figuigis established an inalienable right known as Haq l-ma, the right to water. To ensure the maintenance of the pipelines, the residents agreed to pay a symbolic fee to the municipality, which has committed to providing the oasis with roads, electricity, and infrastructure.

These efforts explain why, until today, the residents believe that the water belongs to them and not to the state. “In the oasis, we were raised to believe that water is precious, that you don’t waste anything, and that you reuse every drop. Over the centuries, this understanding of the resource has evolved into a culture of survival and created a social cohesion that persists to this day,” says Majid Boudia. Even the transition to a municipal city administration in 1994 did not end the social contract. Today, it forms the strongest bulwark against the reform. For Majid and his family, the principle is clear: what has been built communally cannot be privatized.

The Art of Scarcity

The conflict that divides Figuig today centers on a single piece of legislation: Law 83-21. For the authorities, the creation of regional water management companies (SRMs) represents an inevitable modernization of resource management. In the face of growing water scarcity, it is intended to prevent water from being wasted. For the people of Figuig, this represents a brutal break with a system of collective management that has always been regarded as an non-negotiable common good.

This bond has nothing sentimental about it, says Samira Mizbar, a social economist from Figuig. It is contractually regulated and legally unambiguous. 

“The springs that supply Figuig belong to families. This right is enshrined in the official gazette,” the social scientist points out. “Every beneficiary is listed there with their exact share.” 

Fatiha Kadi of the Water Movement believes that this resource comes with a duty to be vigilant: “The fact that we still have water today is no coincidence; it’s because we’ve mastered the art of scarcity. We live in harmony with the rhythm of the water. When it is abundant, we use it; when it becomes scarce, we conserve it.” She points out that the water travels phenomenal distances from the Atlas Mountains to reach this land, where the sky provides only 120 millimeters of rain per year. “Every drop that arrives here is a miracle that has crossed the mountains.“

Even though the SRM is presented as a national project to secure the water supply, doubts remain in the oasis. “We’ve known for centuries how to deal with water scarcity. If the government really wants to secure the water supply, why does it continue to allow the construction of wells and motor pumps?” asks Majid Bouida.

The entire natural balance of the oasis microclimate is at risk of collapsing.

Figuig sits atop an aquifer whose centuries-old balance is now threatened by the combined effects of climate change and overuse. In 2021, a report by the FAO revealed an alarming reality: within fifty years, seventeen of the oasis’s thirty-nine historic springs have dried up. The total available water supply has shrunk significantly—from 300 to 180 liters per second. According to Majid Boudia, this decline is not an inevitable consequence of climate change. “Certainly, climate change and drought play a role, but it is primarily human pressure that is destroying the oasis.”

The Struggle for Control

In 2010, construction began on the Sfissef Dam, 30 kilometers northwest of Figuig, which went into operation in 2015. By creating an illusion of security, it encouraged investment in palm varieties such as Mejhoul, which consume extremely large amounts of water. As soon as the drought had drained the dam, landowners turned en masse to groundwater. In 2021 alone, 1,338 wells were dug.

As the water level drops, an invisible enemy rises from the depths: salt, which could make the oasis gardens infertile for good. “With the loss of control over water, the entire natural balance of the oasis microclimate is at risk of collapsing,” says Boudia.

In fact, the palm groves in many of Morocco’s oases have been transformed into highly simplified agricultural systems as part of a trend of modernization. 

While these may be potentially more productive, they are also more vulnerable to water scarcity.

To appease the Hirak movement, the authorities organized several meetings with its members. They explained that the SRM is a state-owned enterprise that plans neither to privatize nor to increase the prices. But the wording of the law speaks a different language. For example, Article 2 provides for the establishment of a public limited company (SA) under commercial law with an industrial purpose. It is intended to manage water resources in the future. Article 3 specifies that the capital may be opened to the private sector, provided that the state’s stake does not fall below ten percent. 

“An SA is a business,” says Samira Mizbar, arguing that the government wants to turn water into a commodity that is billed. “That’s unacceptable, especially since a large portion of the population can’t afford it.” Faced with this impasse, the protesters have turned to the Kingdom’s Ombudsman’s Office. Even though no tangible results have been achieved so far, giving up is not an option. “Giving up would mean leaving Figuig. And that’s out of the question,” Samira emphasizes.

One Million Minutes of Resistance

The Hirak in Figuig started small. In October 2023, two days before the first vote on the implementation of Law 83-21 in the municipal council, six people demonstrated in front of City Hall. A young photographer live-streamed the sit-in on Facebook. Ultimately, the municipal council voted for joining the controversial SRM by a very narrow majority. Soon after, a sense of having been betrayed by politicians led to the creation of the local coordinating body for advocacy on matters concerning the Figuig oasis.

One of the water movement’s greatest achievements was breaking through Figuig’s geographical isolation by building national support alliances.

A coalition now includes 24 members, among them labor unions, human rights organizations, and feminist movements. 

These supporters gathered at the oasis as part of a solidarity caravan that traveled from Casablanca through several cities to Figuig. They made it clear that Figuig’s problem is not a local dispute, but a matter of sovereignty and human rights. 

Meanwhile, the water movement is making its voice heard at the national level: through a study meeting in the heart of parliament or at major national and international conferences on water scarcity and climate change. On September 26, 2025, the movement reached a staggering milestone: one million minutes of resistance—through sit-ins under the scorching sun or in the bitter cold of the mountains, through nighttime marches by the light of cell phone flashlights, or concerts with cooking pots.

Women are the true driving force: they are resilient, deeply rooted, and ready to do whatever it takes to protect our water.

Women have always been at the forefront of this movement, wearing their traditional white robes. The haïk, which was once reserved for the elderly or for work in the fields, has become a powerful symbol for political communication. The garment serves as a reminder of past struggles, says Fatiha Kadi: “It is an echo of the resistance against colonialism and during the years of the ‘Lead Era.’” The women of Figuig have always been resistance fighters and a role model for all of Morocco, she adds. “By wearing the haïk, they protect their dignity in the face of what they call the new neoliberal colonialism.”

Water in Morocco

  • Morocco is at risk of losing 80 percent of its water resources within the next 25 years.
  • The fill rate of Moroccan reservoirs fell from 61.1 percent to 29.1 percent between 2018 and 2023.
  • 50 percent of Morocco's rainfall is concentrated in just 7 percent of the country's land area, which means that more than 90 percent of the country receives only 50 percent of the rainfall.
  • Morocco plans to make massive investments in desalination – 20 plants are set to be built by 2030.

The role of women in the Figuig Hirak goes beyond their mere numerical presence; they are the true driving force. “I have always compared the women of Figuig to our palm trees,” says Zoubida Benali, a member of the Water Hirak coordination group. “The palm tree is incredibly resilient: it consumes only what is necessary to survive, yet is capable of spreading its roots over incredible distances to absorb even the slightest trace of moisture. The women here are just the same. They are resilient, deeply rooted, and ready to do whatever it takes to protect our water.”

The central role of women can also be explained by a demographic reality. As economic pressure drives men to migrate to the cities, women have become the pillars of the oasis economy—whether through agricultural work or business operations. Fatima Kandar, 63, embodies their perseverance. At the head of a wool cooperative and an association for the protection of cultural heritage, she uses poetry as a lever of resistance. “I’ve never seen the inside of a school, but the words know where to find me. The poems come to me all on their own. Thanks to the Hirak, my voice has been heard everywhere, and it won’t be silenced.”

 A detailed version of the text in French is available on the website of the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s Morocco office.

Rationale                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      Governance has traditionally been associated with legal compliance, fiduciary oversight and accountability to Boards and donors. Yet for many peacebuilding organisations, this understanding is increasingly incomplete. Alongside legal responsibilities sit other forms of accountability to staff, members, partners and communities. Balancing these different accountabilities is rarely straightforward, particularly as organisations seek to strengthen participation, representation and locally led approaches while retaining clear responsibility for organisational decisions. 

These questions are often central to our work with individual partners, yet not easy to engage with as they require a re-allocation of power. An external partner, as well as dedicated funding and attention, can help create the space for such delicate conversations. They also benefit greatly from being supported through peer exchanges, between partner organisations and between Board members themselves.  

Our peer-learning initiative 

As a separate yet complementary initiative to its Organisational Development support, PeaceNexus launched in Q4 of 2021 a board-level peer-learning group. Facilitated by a peer-learning specialist, it provides a safe space where Board members can reflect on their role and how to evolve it in today’s context, as well as receive support and practical suggestions for their immediate challenges.  

An internal review, as well as regular attendance, confirmed the need. It is now an on-going initiative open to PeaceNexus’ current and past international OD partners. 

Small grants and reflection paper 

In 2024, PeaceNexus provided a small grant to six of its partner organisations to support their governance adaptation efforts: Build Up, UNOY, GPPAC, Life and Peace Institute, Conciliation Resources and International Alert.   The report Rethinking governance for mutual accountability: Lessons from six peacebuilding organisations captures their journey as they re-examined their organisational identity and legitimacy, created and held space for difficult governance conversations; and translated these reflections into new governance practice. 

Download the report

Este livro descreve em pormenor a jornada do Acordo de Maputo. Escrito por Mirko Manzoni e Neha Sanghrajka, que apoiaram e facilitaram a mediação e negociação do Acordo, o livro traça passo a passo os esforços meticulosos para construir confiança e credibilidade em circunstâncias muitas vezes desafiantes, com base nas recordações dos próprios autores sobre a mediação e os esforços subsequentes de implementação do Acordo. Perspectivas dos mediadores e de outras pessoas directamente ligadas ao processo dão vida à trajectória única de Moçambique rumo à paz e à reconciliação, bem como à coragem, perseverança e inovação de todos os envolvidos.

Mirko Manzoni, Neha Sanghrajka

TOKYO, JAPAN – 27 OCTOBER 2026 

Community Jameel and C40 Cities today launched the Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners, developed by the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, together with UrbanShift, to support Japan in integrating climate action into its urban development policies.

The launch took place in Tokyo, Japan, at an event co-hosted by Community Jameel and C40 Cities, with a keynote speech delivered by Yuriko Koike, Governor of Tokyo, and the participation of Mohammed Jameel KBE, Founder of Community Jameel. 

With opening remarks by George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, the event also featured a fireside chat between Murali Ram, Regional Director, East, Southeast Asia and Oceania, C40 Cities, and Bridget Smyth, City Architect and Design Director, City of Sydney.

The Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners provides practical guidance for embedding climate action throughout the urban planning process, covering ten common stages of preparing and delivering an urban plan, from initiation and data collection through to policy development, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation.

The guide also sets out key areas where planning policy can support climate action, including flooding, extreme heat and drought, nature, informal settlements, compact and polycentric development, proximity, mode shift and transit-oriented development and sustainable buildings.

Designed for urban planning teams within local governments, including cities with or without a formal climate action plan, the guide supports planners to integrate climate considerations into strategic spatial plans, master plans, land-use plans and related policies.

The Japanese edition includes new forewords from Governor Koike and George Richards, as well as a new case study, developed by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, that highlights Tokyo’s efforts to restructure the city into more walkable neighbourhoods by leveraging the city’s dense rail network, with the aim of ensuring Tokyo’s sustainable development amid major societal changes, including population decline, a declining birthrate, and an aging population. 

The case study also considers how this approach can reduce CO2 emissions from transport and support greener, lower-energy urban development.

Yuriko Koike, Governor of Tokyo, said: “Promoting urban resilience and decarbonisation to protect people’s lives and livelihoods is our responsibility. 

“Tokyo is stepping up its preparations for increasingly severe natural disasters, including flood control measures such as massive underground tunnels that temporarily store river water and rainwater caused by heavy rainfall. 

“Moreover, with a population of 14 million, Tokyo is a major consumer of energy. We will contribute to global decarbonisation by actively adopting innovative technologies, such as aiming to deploy Air Solar, a next-generation solar cell developed in Japan, and install gigawatt-class floating offshore wind farms. 

“Enhancing urban sustainability through such measures is essential not only in responding to climate change, but also from the perspective of energy security. 

“I hope that cities, countries, and the many other stakeholders around the world will stand together ever more closely, and that our progress towards a world where everyone can live with peace of mind will grow stronger still.”

George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, said: “Urban planning plays a critical role in determining how cities respond to climate change, from the way neighbourhoods grow to how people move, where development takes place and how communities are protected from climate risks. 

“The new Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners will expand access to this practical resource, supporting efforts to translate climate commitments into the policies and plans that shape urban development in cities across Japan.”

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: “Transforming climate targets into everyday spatial policies requires actionable, grounded tools for city planners. This Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners provides precisely that framework. 

“Tokyo, under Governor Koike's leadership, continues to set a strong benchmark through its zero-emission strategies and climate adaptation policies, and we are proud to collaborate with the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and Community Jameel to support cities across Japan in building safer, sustainable, and low-carbon urban futures.”

The Japanese edition comes as cities across Japan respond to growing climate pressures. In Tokyo, the Metropolitan Government’s Climate Change Adaptation Plan and other initiatives address risks including rising temperatures, extreme heat, heavy rainfall, and flooding, alongside measures to strengthen the city’s resilience.

Tokyo is also pursuing significant emissions reductions through its Zero Emission Tokyo Strategy, under which the Metropolitan Government has set a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 60% from 2000 levels by 2035, alongside its goal of achieving zero emissions by 2050.

Tokyo is among 33 cities participating in the C40 and UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, a global platform supporting cities to embed climate-responsive and equitable planning principles into master plans and land-use regulations by 2035. 

Announced at the 2025 Local Leaders Forum in Rio de Janeiro ahead of COP30 in Belém, Brazil, the Urban Planning Accelerator brings together cities committed to strengthening the role of urban planning in reducing emissions, protecting communities from climate risks, restoring ecosystems, and creating more inclusive and liveable cities.

The Accelerator builds on the work of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel that has supported climate-responsive urban planning in Amman, Jordan, and Chennai, India. 

Across both cities, the Labs have contributed to 15 planning policies, regulations, strategies, and statutory planning instruments, with these initiatives, directly reaching 4.5 million people.

The Labs have also developed practical methodologies and tools to support cities in integrating climate action into urban planning, including climate risk mapping, emissions and land-use modelling, and zoning reform templates.

These approaches will continue to support cities participating in the Urban Planning Accelerator as they work to translate climate commitments into planning policies, regulations, and development controls. 

The Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners will serve as one of the resources available to cities through this process, supporting planners to connect climate goals with the decisions that shape how cities develop.

コミュニティ・ジャミールとC40、小池百合子東京都知事とともに「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」日本語版を発表

2026年10月27日 日本・東京

コミュニティ・ジャミールとC40（C40都市気候リーダーシップグループ）は本日、ジャミールC40都市計画気候ラボ（Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs）がアーバンシフト（Urban　Shift）と共同で策定した「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」の日本語版を発表しました。本ガイドは、日本において都市開発政策に気候変動対策を組み込む取り組みを支援するものです。

発表は、コミュニティ・ジャミールとC40の共催により日本・東京で開催されたイベントにて行われ、東京都知事　小池百合子氏による基調講演が行われ、コミュニティ・ジャミール創設者のモハメッド・ジャミール・KBEが出席しました。イベントでは、コミュニティ・ジャミールのディレクターであるジョージ・リチャーズによる開会挨拶に続き、C40東・東南アジア・オセアニア地域ディレクターのムラリ・ラムと、シドニー市シティ・アーキテクト兼デザイン・ディレクターのブリジット・スマイスによる対談も行われました。

「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」は、都市計画プロセス全体に気候変動対策を組み込むための実践的な指針を示すものです。計画の立案開始やデータ収集から、政策策定、実施、モニタリング、評価に至るまで、都市計画の策定・実施における一般的な都市計画の流れを10の段階に分け、網羅しています。

また本ガイドでは、洪水、猛暑と干ばつ、自然環境、非公認居住地、コンパクトかつ多核的な都市開発、生活圏の近接性、交通手段の転換と公共交通指向型開発（TOD）、持続可能な建築物など、都市計画政策が気候変動対策を後押しできる重点分野を示しています。

本ガイドは、正式な気候行動計画の有無にかかわらず、地方自治体の都市計画担当チームを対象としており、計画担当者が戦略的空間計画、マスタープラン、土地利用計画および関連政策に気候変動の観点を組み込むことを支援します。

日本語版には、小池都知事およびジョージ・リチャーズによる新たな序文に加え、東京都の取り組み事例も新たに収録されています。この取り組みでは、人口減少や少子高齢化といった大きな社会変化の中で東京の持続可能な発展を確保することを目指し、稠密な鉄道網を活用し、歩いて暮らせるまちづくりを図っていることを紹介しています。また、こうした取り組みが交通由来のCO2排出量の削減や、より環境に優しく省エネルギーな都市開発にどのように寄与し得るかについても紹介されています。

小池百合子 東京都知事は次のように述べています。

「都民の生命と暮らしを守るため、都市の強靭化と脱炭素化を推進することは私たちの責務です。東京では、大雨による河川の水や雨水を一時的に貯留する巨大な地下トンネルなどの治水対策をはじめ、激甚化する自然災害への備えを強化しています。」

「また、1,400万人の人口を抱える東京は、エネルギーの大消費地でもあります。日本で開発された次世代型太陽電池「Air Solar」の普及や、ギガワット級の浮体式洋上風力発電の導入を目指すなど、革新的な技術を積極的に取り入れることで、世界の脱炭素化に貢献してまいります。」

「こうした取り組みを通じて都市のサステナビリティを高めることは、気候変動への対応のみならず、エネルギー安全保障の観点からも不可欠です。世界の都市、国々、そして多くのステークホルダーの皆様がこれまで以上に固く連携し、誰もが安心して暮らせる世界に向けた歩みがさらに力強いものとなることを願っています。」

コミュニティ・ジャミールのディレクター、ジョージ・リチャーズは次のように述べています。

「都市計画は、地域の成長のあり方から、人々の移動手段、開発の場所、そして気候リスクからのコミュニティの保護に至るまで、都市が気候変動にどう対応するかを左右する重要な役割を担っています。『都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド』の新たな日本語版は、この実践的なガイドブックをより多くの方々に届け、日本各地の都市において、気候変動に関する目標を都市開発の方向性を定める政策や計画へと落とし込む取り組みの一助となることを期待します。」

C40のエグゼクティブ・ディレクター、マーク・ワッツは次のように述べています。

「気候目標を日々の空間政策へと転換するには、都市計画担当者にとって実行可能で現場に根差したツールが必要です。『都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド』の日本語版は、まさにその枠組みを提供するものです。小池都知事のリーダーシップのもと、東京はゼロエミッション戦略や気候変動適応策を通じて、引き続き模範となる取り組みを示しています。私たちは、東京都およびコミュニティ・ジャミールと協力し、日本各地の都市がより安全で持続可能な低炭素の未来を築くことを支援できることを誇りに思います。」

今回の日本語版の発表は、日本各地の都市が高まる気候変動の圧力への対応を進める中で行われました。東京では、都の気候変動適応計画をはじめとする取り組みにより、気温上昇、猛暑、豪雨、洪水などのリスクに対処するとともに、都市のレジリエンスを強化する施策が講じられています。

また東京は「ゼロエミッション東京戦略」を通じて大幅な排出削減を進めており、2050年までに排出ゼロを達成するという目標とあわせて、2035年までに温室効果ガス排出量を2000年比で60%以上削減するという目標を掲げています。

東京は、C40と国連人間居住計画（UN-Habitat）による「都市計画アクセラレーター（Urban Planning Accelerator）」に参加する33都市の一つです。同アクセラレーターは、2035年までに気候変動に対応した公正な計画原則をマスタープランや土地利用規制に組み込むよう都市を支援するグローバルなプラットフォームです。ブラジル・ベレンで開催されたCOP30に先立ち、2025年にリオデジャネイロで開催されたローカルリーダーズフォーラムで発表された都市計画アクセラレーターは、排出削減、気候リスクからのコミュニティの保護、生態系の回復、そしてより包摂的で住みやすい都市の創出において、都市計画の役割を強化することに取り組む都市を結集しています。

同アクセラレーターは、C40とコミュニティ・ジャミールのパートナーシップであるジャミールC40都市計画気候ラボの取り組みを基盤としています。同ラボは、ヨルダンのアンマンとインドのチェンナイにおいて、気候変動に対応した都市計画を支援してきました。両都市において、同ラボは15件の計画政策、規制、戦略、法定計画手段の策定に貢献しており、これらの取り組みは450万人に直接届いています。

また同ラボは、気候リスクマッピング、排出量および土地利用のモデリング、ゾーニング改革のテンプレートなど、都市計画に気候変動対策を組み込む都市を支援するための実践的な手法やツールも開発してきました。

これらのアプローチは今後も、都市計画アクセラレーターに参加する都市が気候変動に関する公約を計画政策、規制、開発管理へと落とし込む取り組みを支援していきます。「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」は、このプロセスにおいて都市が活用できるリソースの一つとして、気候目標と都市の発展を形づくる意思決定とを結びつける計画担当者の取り組みを支援します。
items.title: Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate LabsCommunity Jameel and C40 Cities launch Japanese edition of Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners with Yuriko Koike, Governor of Tokyo27 October 2026
items.summary:
TOKYO, JAPAN – 27 OCTOBER 2026 

Community Jameel and C40 Cities today launched the Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners, developed by the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, together with UrbanShift, to support Japan in integrating climate action into its urban development policies.

The launch took place in Tokyo, Japan, at an event co-hosted by Community Jameel and C40 Cities, with a keynote speech delivered by Yuriko Koike, Governor of Tokyo, and the participation of Mohammed Jameel KBE, Founder of Community Jameel. 

With opening remarks by George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, the event also featured a fireside chat between Murali Ram, Regional Director, East, Southeast Asia and Oceania, C40 Cities, and Bridget Smyth, City Architect and Design Director, City of Sydney.

The Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners provides practical guidance for embedding climate action throughout the urban planning process, covering ten common stages of preparing and delivering an urban plan, from initiation and data collection through to policy development, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation.

The guide also sets out key areas where planning policy can support climate action, including flooding, extreme heat and drought, nature, informal settlements, compact and polycentric development, proximity, mode shift and transit-oriented development and sustainable buildings.

Designed for urban planning teams within local governments, including cities with or without a formal climate action plan, the guide supports planners to integrate climate considerations into strategic spatial plans, master plans, land-use plans and related policies.

The Japanese edition includes new forewords from Governor Koike and George Richards, as well as a new case study, developed by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government, that highlights Tokyo’s efforts to restructure the city into more walkable neighbourhoods by leveraging the city’s dense rail network, with the aim of ensuring Tokyo’s sustainable development amid major societal changes, including population decline, a declining birthrate, and an aging population. 

The case study also considers how this approach can reduce CO2 emissions from transport and support greener, lower-energy urban development.

Yuriko Koike, Governor of Tokyo, said: “Promoting urban resilience and decarbonisation to protect people’s lives and livelihoods is our responsibility. 

“Tokyo is stepping up its preparations for increasingly severe natural disasters, including flood control measures such as massive underground tunnels that temporarily store river water and rainwater caused by heavy rainfall. 

“Moreover, with a population of 14 million, Tokyo is a major consumer of energy. We will contribute to global decarbonisation by actively adopting innovative technologies, such as aiming to deploy Air Solar, a next-generation solar cell developed in Japan, and install gigawatt-class floating offshore wind farms. 

“Enhancing urban sustainability through such measures is essential not only in responding to climate change, but also from the perspective of energy security. 

“I hope that cities, countries, and the many other stakeholders around the world will stand together ever more closely, and that our progress towards a world where everyone can live with peace of mind will grow stronger still.”

George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, said: “Urban planning plays a critical role in determining how cities respond to climate change, from the way neighbourhoods grow to how people move, where development takes place and how communities are protected from climate risks. 

“The new Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners will expand access to this practical resource, supporting efforts to translate climate commitments into the policies and plans that shape urban development in cities across Japan.”

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: “Transforming climate targets into everyday spatial policies requires actionable, grounded tools for city planners. This Japanese edition of the Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners provides precisely that framework. 

“Tokyo, under Governor Koike's leadership, continues to set a strong benchmark through its zero-emission strategies and climate adaptation policies, and we are proud to collaborate with the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and Community Jameel to support cities across Japan in building safer, sustainable, and low-carbon urban futures.”

The Japanese edition comes as cities across Japan respond to growing climate pressures. In Tokyo, the Metropolitan Government’s Climate Change Adaptation Plan and other initiatives address risks including rising temperatures, extreme heat, heavy rainfall, and flooding, alongside measures to strengthen the city’s resilience.

Tokyo is also pursuing significant emissions reductions through its Zero Emission Tokyo Strategy, under which the Metropolitan Government has set a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 60% from 2000 levels by 2035, alongside its goal of achieving zero emissions by 2050.

Tokyo is among 33 cities participating in the C40 and UN-Habitat Urban Planning Accelerator, a global platform supporting cities to embed climate-responsive and equitable planning principles into master plans and land-use regulations by 2035. 

Announced at the 2025 Local Leaders Forum in Rio de Janeiro ahead of COP30 in Belém, Brazil, the Urban Planning Accelerator brings together cities committed to strengthening the role of urban planning in reducing emissions, protecting communities from climate risks, restoring ecosystems, and creating more inclusive and liveable cities.

The Accelerator builds on the work of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel that has supported climate-responsive urban planning in Amman, Jordan, and Chennai, India. 

Across both cities, the Labs have contributed to 15 planning policies, regulations, strategies, and statutory planning instruments, with these initiatives, directly reaching 4.5 million people.

The Labs have also developed practical methodologies and tools to support cities in integrating climate action into urban planning, including climate risk mapping, emissions and land-use modelling, and zoning reform templates.

These approaches will continue to support cities participating in the Urban Planning Accelerator as they work to translate climate commitments into planning policies, regulations, and development controls. 

The Climate Action Guide for Urban Planners will serve as one of the resources available to cities through this process, supporting planners to connect climate goals with the decisions that shape how cities develop.

2026年10月27日 日本・東京

コミュニティ・ジャミールとC40（C40都市気候リーダーシップグループ）は本日、ジャミールC40都市計画気候ラボ（Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs）がアーバンシフト（Urban　Shift）と共同で策定した「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」の日本語版を発表しました。本ガイドは、日本において都市開発政策に気候変動対策を組み込む取り組みを支援するものです。

発表は、コミュニティ・ジャミールとC40の共催により日本・東京で開催されたイベントにて行われ、東京都知事　小池百合子氏による基調講演が行われ、コミュニティ・ジャミール創設者のモハメッド・ジャミール・KBEが出席しました。イベントでは、コミュニティ・ジャミールのディレクターであるジョージ・リチャーズによる開会挨拶に続き、C40東・東南アジア・オセアニア地域ディレクターのムラリ・ラムと、シドニー市シティ・アーキテクト兼デザイン・ディレクターのブリジット・スマイスによる対談も行われました。

「都市計画担当者のための気候行動ガイド」は、都市計画プロセス全体に気候変動対策を組み込むための実践的な指針を示すものです。計画の立案開始やデータ収集から、政策策定、実施、モニタリング、評価に至るまで、都市計画の策定・実施における一般的な都市計画の流れを10の段階に分け、網羅しています。

また本ガイドでは、洪水、猛暑と干ばつ、自然環境、非公認居住地、コンパクトかつ多核的な都市開発、生活圏の近接性、交通手段の転換と公共交通指向型開発（TOD）、持続可能な建築物など、都市計画政策が気候変動対策を後押しできる重点分野を示しています。

本ガイドは、正式な気候行動計画の有無にかかわらず、地方自治体の都市計画担当チームを対象としており、計画担当者が戦略的空間計画、マスタープラン、土地利用計画および関連政策に気候変動の観点を組み込むことを支援します。

日本語版には、小池都知事およびジョージ・リチャーズによる新たな序文に加え、東京都の取り組み事例も新たに収録されています。この取り組みでは、人口減少や少子高齢化といった大きな社会変化の中で東京の持続可能な発展を確保することを目指し、稠密な鉄道網を活用し、歩いて暮らせるまちづくりを図っていることを紹介しています。また、こうした取り組みが交通由来のCO2排出量の削減や、より環境に優しく省エネルギーな都市開発にどのように寄与し得るかについても紹介されています。

「都民の生命と暮らしを守るため、都市の強靭化と脱炭素化を推進することは私たちの責務です。東京では、大雨による河川の水や雨水を一時的に貯留する巨大な地下トンネルなどの治水対策をはじめ、激甚化する自然災害への備えを強化しています。」

「こうした取り組みを通じて都市のサステナビリティを高めることは、気候変動への対応のみならず、エネルギー安全保障の観点からも不可欠です。世界の都市、国々、そして多くのステークホルダーの皆様がこれまで以上に固く連携し、誰もが安心して暮らせる世界に向けた歩みがさらに力強いものとなることを願っています。」

The interview with Jan-Niclas Gesenhues was conducted by Kristin Funke.

Kristin Funke: Why is the biodiversity conference important to you, and what are your expectations as you head to Yerevan?

Jan-Niclas Gesenhues: The CBD demonstrates that international law and multilateralism are alive and well. I think that’s extremely important in these times, when people like Trump are trampling on international law. The biodiversity COPs have consistently shown that the international community can reach agreement on issues. Conservation can serve as a unifying force, especially now, to protect our shared home.

And conservation is not just an end in itself: Health, food security for many people worldwide, and the economy are at stake here. Pollination by insects, birds, and other animals secures agricultural yields worldwide worth up to nearly 600 billion US dollars per year. This is not something that can be replaced by technical solutions. 

At the same time, conservation helps prevent pandemics and is a key to disease control. About 70 percent of cancer drugs, for example, are derived from natural substances or are modeled after them. In addition, there is the huge impact on climate protection. So there are plenty of good reasons to better protect our global biodiversity, and the COPs are the tool for doing so.

What specific demands are you taking with you to COP17? What are the most important points from your perspective?

One of the most important tasks is to secure global funding for biodiversity conservation. Industrialized countries have pledged 30 billion dollars per year through 2030 to so-called developing countries, but so far we are still far from reaching that target. This is a major issue of credibility, especially with regard to our partners in the Global South. I expect the German government to honor its commitments to provide 6 billion euros in climate finance and 1.5 billion euros in biodiversity finance per year. But a few days ago, it came to light that Germany is currently breaking its promises. In doing so, the government is severely damaging Germany’s credibility around the world.

A second key demand is that we make real progress toward achieving the 30x30 goal and protect 30 percent of land and marine areas by 2030. A new study by Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean says that if we truly implement the existing pledges made by individual countries, we can reach 27 percent by 2030. This is a great sign, especially in these times, that goals agreed upon under international law are achievable. That’s exactly what the CBD COP demonstrates. I believe it is absolutely essential to support implementation in Yerevan. 

The third important point, in my view, is that the Cali Fund becomes operational and is implemented, because this is a matter of justice. It’s unacceptable that European or American pharmaceutical or cosmetic companies earn billions by exploiting biodiversity while Indigenous peoples and local communities are left empty-handed. The Cali Fund is intended to receive contributions from industry, pharmaceutical companies and cosmetics companies, with the funds specifically allocated to supporting the countries and communities from which these resources originate. This global benefit-sharing system must work. This is a fundamental question of justice, and the Yerevan COP must follow through on it.

More on the UN Biodiversity Conference

This article is part of the Heinrich Böll Foundation’s coverage of the UN Biodiversity Conferences (CBD COP). Explore analyses, commentaries and background information on past and ongoing negotiations, key debates and outcomes.

➤ Explore our CBD COP dossier

Progress toward achieving the targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), which was adopted in 2022, is still very limited. We are now halfway to 2030. Where do we need to act on a global level to achieve these goals? 

If we do not meet the targets by 2030, the cost of necessary measures to combat biodiversity loss will double. At the same time, food is becoming more expensive, extreme weather events are becoming more severe, and diseases and crop failures are becoming more frequent. That’s why it’s so important that we follow through on our global goals now. Things are looking pretty good for the 30x30 goal on land, but not so much in the oceans. Yet the oceans are an extremely important source of food and a treasure trove of biodiversity. That’s why it’s crucial that the upcoming first Conference of the Parties to the BBNJ Agreement – the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction – be a success, so that we can achieve the 30x30 goal in the oceans as well.

The second issue here is the severe pollution caused by chemicals and plastic, which is one of the main drivers of biodiversity loss. There is an important goal in the GBF that aims to halve the harmful effects of toxic inputs on the natural environment. The international community needs to make progress in this area, and Europe, for example, can now deliver concrete results with the process to ban certain PFAS – the so-called “forever chemicals”. 

Another important goal is the elimination of environmentally harmful subsidies. One thing I would abolish immediately would be tax breaks for gas and oil in plastic production. These are extremely harmful to the environment. These three points – reducing toxic impacts, phasing out environmentally harmful subsidies and protecting marine biodiversity – are important GBF goals where I expect progress from the COP.

You have already mentioned the fossil fuel industry as a driver of biodiversity loss; who else do you see playing a role here? How can we counteract these drivers, both globally and here in Germany? 

The main causes of biodiversity loss are habitat loss and toxic substances in the environment. Habitat loss is largely due to the extraction of raw materials and industrialized agriculture. That’s why, in my view, these are the areas where we need to focus our efforts. We must stop extracting raw materials from nature, using them once, and then disposing of them back into nature. That’s simply not sustainable. What’s needed globally is a true circular economy; this is extremely important for biodiversity. So, we need to replace raw material extraction with a true circular economy, and replace industrialized agriculture with small-scale, organic farming, accompanied by a more sustainable diet and a reduction in pesticide use. 

Another point: Conservation alone is no longer enough. In addition to designating protected areas, the most important thing is that we now embark on a decade of restoration. This doesn’t even necessarily have to result in protected areas. The goal would be to restore developed waterways to a more natural state, remove paving from sealed areas, and restore forests to a state closer to nature. That is at least as important as designating protected areas.

What are Alliance 90/The Greens’ policy proposals regarding conservation and biodiversity in Germany? 

In my view, our most important demand is that the German government honor its international financial commitments: one billion euros for the TFFF global rainforest fund, 6 billion euros in climate finance, and 1.5 billion euros in biodiversity finance. The government is falling short, and that is why we are pushing for this to be corrected and for the promises to be kept. We have just submitted a major motion to the Bundestag in which we list, in very specific terms and by budget line, where funding needs to be increased – particularly in the budget of the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), because that is where most of the funds for global climate and biodiversity finance are allocated. And we are doing everything we can to ensure that the CDU does not succeed in blocking TFFF funding.

The second demand is that the government follow through on and strengthen the implementation of the national biodiversity strategy. Germany must also meet the 30 percent target, but it is still 17 percent short of the required land area. The government must also consistently implement the EU Nature Restoration Regulation – that is, the Nature Restoration Law. 80 percent of Europe’s ecosystems are in poor condition. In Germany, more than 95 percent of the bogs and wetlands have been destroyed and drained. What is needed here is a broad-based restoration program, as well as a significant increase in funding for the Federal Action Plan on Nature-based Solutions for Climate and Biodiversity (ANK) and the nature conservation fund. This would also benefit local communities and farms, as it would lead to better water management on their land and greater soil biodiversity, which ultimately helps ensure good harvests. Restoration is not only about nature conservation; it also benefits agriculture, flood protection, public health, and the quality of life in our cities. In this regard, the government needs to do much more than it has so far.

Projects at the municipal or regional level clearly demonstrate that this can work. There are already a number of successful examples.

Yes, I’m really happy to see that. When we were in the federal government, we fought hard to get the ANK passed despite massive opposition, and now it’s here. My heart fills with joy every time I see the Aasee being restored to its natural state back home in Ibbenbüren. Or that 75 ANK projects were implemented in Bremen – a number that is far disproportionate to the state’s size and financial resources. From formerly paved areas where urban gardening and neighborhood initiatives have now found a home, to large-scale wetland restoration projects and species conservation programs in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the lesser spotted eagle population is finally stabilizing again and, at the same time, many wonderful natural areas and habitats are being restored – that’s where I see the fruits of our hard work. Seeing that the political decisions we’ve made actually lead to tangible results – and don’t just remain abstract – is so valuable and really feels good. 

In the policy paper you recently co-authored with Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak, you advocate a new conservation agenda and argue that large-scale private investment, innovative businesses and new business models are also needed to drive major conservation projects. How can this work when previous experience with biodiversity banks, certificates, offset credits, and other financial market-based instruments shows that they are fraught with risks and inherent contradictions and have not yielded any significant successes in biodiversity conservation? 

The GBF makes it very clear that we simply cannot cover this enormous funding requirement for biodiversity conservation with tax revenue alone. Governments don’t have enough money for that. We need public funds, philanthropic foundations, but also funding from the private sector. On the one hand, there are mandatory contributions – through the Cali Fund, for example – to compensate countries and Indigenous communities when companies profit from biodiversity. 

On the other, there are incentives for companies to invest in biodiversity. We can’t do it without these resources, which is why I find the idea of seeking out allies for biodiversity conservation – ones that are perhaps not immediately obvious – quite exciting. Food retailers, for example, who say, “We don’t want dubious carbon credits; we want to offset our carbon footprint through peatland restoration in Europe.” Or chocolate and rubber producers who know that they must invest in biodiversity throughout their supply chains because their business models depend on it. There are various approaches. Some companies are investing in the resilience of their supply chains. Others ask how conservation work can create enough buzz to boost sales. One example is the significant economic impact of national parks around the world. Especially in lower-income countries, nature-based tourism generates revenue and creates jobs. I don’t have a problem with companies making money from birdwatching trips – as long as nature benefits from it and the local community is involved.

Finally, and this is something forward-thinking companies are telling us, too, we need regulatory frameworks. We cannot allow the Green Deal to be rolled back now, thereby penalizing the very companies that are leading the way. We need supply chain resilience, biodiversity-centered business models, and regulatory frameworks that enhance the competitive position of companies at the forefront of biodiversity efforts. In my opinion, those are the three components we need. If the right incentives and regulatory framework are in place, the private sector can also be an important player – at least those parts of the private sector that are no longer willing to base their business models solely on the destruction of nature, but have recognized that they can sustain their businesses only by taking action to protect biodiversity. We should stand behind business leaders who are calling for the Deforestation Directive, the Supply Chain Act, and the Restoration Regulation to remain in place.

Apart from the CBD, which international forums and initiatives do you consider relevant or promising for the protection of biodiversity? 

First, I’d like to mention two more multilateral processes, because they’re absolutely crucial. First, the BBNJ Agreement, which addresses the conservation of marine biodiversity in the high seas, because it appears to have the strongest enforcement mechanisms of any global agreement and is the only one that designates specific protected areas. The parties to it can make decisions by a qualified majority; unanimity is not required. I have high hopes for the BBNJ Agreement. Second, I expect the German government to make a new attempt to advance global negotiations on a plastic reduction agreement. In my view, qualified majorities are the way to go here as well. We cannot allow ourselves to be held hostage by individual oil-producing countries with fossil-fuel-based business models. 

But aside from the multilateral forums, I would like to highlight the International Indigenous Forum on Biodiversity. It’s holding its own global gathering of Indigenous peoples and local communities, focusing on issues such as reconciling the strengthening of Indigenous land rights and biodiversity conservation. I think that’s extremely relevant. 

Another thing to keep an eye on is the annual meetings of IPBES – the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services – because a lot has happened there. I find it really exciting that IPBES has now teamed up with social scientists, because they’ve recognized that scientific knowledge alone isn’t enough – we also need a political plan for implementation. Who are our allies? Who are the key players? When is the timing right? It’s almost a cliché by now, but the issue isn’t a lack of scientific knowledge, we just need to put what we know into practice. 

My favorite instruments are actually the bilateral biodiversity partnerships, or NBSAP Accelerator Partnerships. When I was parliamentary state secretary, I traveled to Cali and Rome with founding documents and, together with 10 to 15 countries – from Armenia to Colombia to Somalia – launched such biodiversity partnerships. There’s an incredible amount of potential here, because it really comes down to this: How do we put this into practice? Where do I designate a protected area? What does a protected area ordinance look like? What other programs can I establish? What kind of capacity building do I need for this? How do I involve local communities? That’s where conservation really comes into play, and I believe that we in Germany have a lot to offer with our expertise in protected area management – but conversely, there is also an incredible amount that we can learn. That’s where national park rangers from Rwanda and Germany get together and exchange practical insights as equals. That’s what I think is so brilliant about this instrument. It’s something we urgently need to strengthen and expand.

Ahead of the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) in Armenia, we speak with Green Party member of the German Bundestag Jan-Niclas Gesenhues about nature conservation, funding gaps, the role of business and international cooperation. This is not something that can be replaced by technical solutions. 

At the same time, conservation helps prevent pandemics and is a key to disease control. About 70 percent of cancer drugs, for example, are derived from natural substances or are modeled after them. In addition, there is the huge impact on climate protection. So there are plenty of good reasons to better protect our global biodiversity, and the COPs are the tool for doing so.

What specific demands are you taking with you to COP17? What are the most important points from your perspective?

One of the most important tasks is to secure global funding for biodiversity conservation. Industrialized countries have pledged 30 billion dollars per year through 2030 to so-called developing countries, but so far we are still far from reaching that target. This is a major issue of credibility, especially with regard to our partners in the Global South. I expect the German government to honor its commitments to provide 6 billion euros in climate finance and 1.5 billion euros in biodiversity finance per year. But a few days ago, it came to light that Germany is currently breaking its promises. In doing so, the government is severely damaging Germany’s credibility around the world.

A second key demand is that we make real progress toward achieving the 30x30 goal and protect 30 percent of land and marine areas by 2030. A new study by Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean says that if we truly implement the existing pledges made by individual countries, we can reach 27 percent by 2030. This is a great sign, especially in these times, that goals agreed upon under international law are achievable. That’s exactly what the CBD COP demonstrates. I believe it is absolutely essential to support implementation in Yerevan. 

The third important point, in my view, is that the Cali Fund becomes operational and is implemented, because this is a matter of justice. It’s unacceptable that European or American pharmaceutical or cosmetic companies earn billions by exploiting biodiversity while Indigenous peoples and local communities are left empty-handed. The Cali Fund is intended to receive contributions from industry, pharmaceutical companies and cosmetics companies, with the funds specifically allocated to supporting the countries and communities from which these resources originate. This global benefit-sharing system must work. This is a fundamental question of justice, and the Yerevan COP must follow through on it.

The second issue here is the severe pollution caused by chemicals and plastic, which is one of the main drivers of biodiversity loss. The international community needs to make progress in this area, and Europe, for example, can now deliver concrete results with the process to ban certain PFAS – the so-called “forever chemicals”. 

Another important goal is the elimination of environmentally harmful subsidies. One thing I would abolish immediately would be tax breaks for gas and oil in plastic production.
