ANTAKYA, TÜRKIYE – 22 OCTOBER 2026

Shapla Hotel, a short documentary about a single mother running a roadside hotel in rural south-west Bangladesh, premiered at the 2026 Antakya International Film Festival, where it was a finalist in the ‘International Documentary Short’ category.

Directed by Roanna Rahman and produced by Community Jameel, the film follows its protagonist, Moyna Begum, as she struggles to keep her hotel running in a region on the front line of the changing climate. 

Shapla Hotel has been honoured at two film festivals in West Bengal, winning awards in the Documentary and Film on Women categories at the 2025 Sundarban International Film Festival. It was also officially selected for the 2026 Bengal International Short Film Festival.  

The film’s trailer was released today and is available to watch online.

A story of resilience

More than 30 million people live in south-west Bangladesh, a low-lying region increasingly exposed to cyclones and record-breaking heatwaves that threaten lives, livelihoods, and water and food security.

Shapla, the water-lily that gives the film its title, is the national flower of Bangladesh. Celebrated for its beauty and its resilience in the harshest conditions, the flower also gives its name to Moyna’s elder daughter.

That same resilience animates Moyna, who operates her hotel in Baradal Bazar in Bangladesh’s Khulna district. 

With no source of running water, she depends on the generosity of neighbours and pays the high prices charged by water vendors. 

Through her everyday encounters, the film reveals a microcosm of a community facing adversity and determined to endure.

Roanna Rahman, the film's director, said: "I met Moyna apa at her hotel. We would have lunch at her place every day while we were filming. 

“People came from everywhere to eat there because the food was so delicious. I was struck by how she managed to run the entire hotel on her own and with so much love. 

“While bustling about, she manages to carry her family and her community on her shoulders, even with all its precarity. 

“I wanted to film her not as a victim of her circumstance but as someone whose strength and humour endures in spite of it."

Building climate resilience in south-west Bangladesh

The film is set in the region where the Jameel Observatory – Climate Resilience Early Warning Systems Network (CREWSnet) – an initiative co-founded by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Community Jameel – is working in partnership with BRAC, an international non-governmental organisation founded in Bangladesh, the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL), and other partners.

The threats posed by climate change – rising sea levels and more extreme weather – mean that people living in this region are likely to face similar crises in the years ahead.

In addition to cyclones, extreme heat is a growing threat, putting people at risk of dehydration and heatstroke.

Children are particularly affected. In 2024, the United Nations in Bangladesh found that heatwaves caused nationwide school closures for two weeks.

In some districts, schools were closed for six to eight weeks due to the combined impact of heatwaves and flooding.

The Jameel Observatory CREWSnet is developing and deploying novel technologies and approaches in south-west Bangladesh to help people manage the dangerous threats posed by climate change.

These include the development of the first Adaptation Fortress, a novel shelter designed to protect communities from extreme heat and tropical storm, which opened earlier this year at the Baradal Aftab Uddin Collegiate School in the Satkhira district. 

The choice of location and shelter design were directly informed by climate modelling by the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet team at MIT. 

Nathaniel Daudrich, Head of Product at Community Jameel and a producer of Shapla Hotel, said: "More than 30 million people in south-west Bangladesh are living with cyclones, flooding, and extreme heat, growing more severe each year. 

“Moyna Begum, Shapla Hotel’s hero, finds the same resilience as the Shapla water-lily, and is a quiet reminder of why the work of the Jameel Observatory-CREWSnet matters so urgently."

A second Adaptation Fortress is under development at Satbaria High School in the Jashore district. 

If the pilot sites prove successful, the initiative will pave the way to scaling up to 1,250 Adaptation Fortresses, providing heatwave relief to half a million of the region’s most vulnerable residents.

GENEVA, SWITZERLAND – 22 OCTOBER 2026

A consortium of global humanitarian and development funders launched a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Humanitarian Working Group to help coordinate how AI can be used safely and effectively in humanitarian emergencies, Community Jameel announced today in Geneva, Switzerland, at the 2026 edition of AidEx, the world’s leading humanitarian aid and disaster relief event.

Jointly led by Community Jameel and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) in collaboration with the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) and the German development agency, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), the Working Group is part of the AI for Development (AI4D) Funders Collaborative, a global partnership of development funders dedicated to unite with partners around the world to centre challenges in the Global South and combat technological and social inequality by supporting inclusive, responsible AI made by and for communities.

Uzma Sulaiman, Associate Director of Community Jameel, announced the AI and Humanitarian Working Group during a panel at AidEx that brought together humanitarian organisations and funders, including FCDO, Enhancing Learning and Research for Humanitarian Assistance, Itad and NSDation Syria.

The new Working Group is launched as AI tools are increasingly being applied across humanitarian response, including in weather forecasting, rapid damage assessment, and other areas of technological innovation, while also raising risks around data privacy, surveillance, and the use of emerging technologies in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

The Working Group will provide a coordination role in assessing how AI is currently being used across the humanitarian sector, which will help to identify opportunities and risks and generate research and evidence to support policymakers and humanitarian organisations in the safe deployment of AI for conflict-affected populations. 

Uzma Sulaiman, Associate Director of Community Jameel, said: “Artificial intelligence has the potential to strengthen humanitarian response, from forecasting and early warning to assessing needs following crises. 

“At the same time, its use in fragile and conflict-affected settings raises important questions around safety, privacy, and accountability. 

“Through the new AI and Humanitarian Working Group, we want to help coordinate with key partners on the responsible use of AI for communities affected by conflict and crisis.”

This Working Group builds on other successes of the AI4D Funders Collaborative and the wider AI4D programme. In 2025, Community Jameel, FCDO, and IDRC launched a flagship AI4D initiative, the AI Evidence Alliance for Social Impact (AEASI), led by the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) and IDinsight, to evaluate and scale AI applications for social impact. 

AEASI is part of J-PAL’s wider evidence and AI portfolio, which also includes Project AI Evidence (PAIE), with USD 7 million from Community Jameel, IDRC, FCDO, Google.org, and Amazon Web Services, and the USD 60 million Evidence for AI in Health (EVAH) initiative, funded by Wellcome, the Gates Foundation, and the Novo Nordisk Foundation and delivered by J-PAL in partnership with the African Population and Health Research Center.

Mike Baily, Senior Advisor, AI, at J-PAL Global, said: "J-PAL welcomes efforts to build more evidence on how and where AI is improving people's livelihoods worldwide. Through AI4D and our wider AI evidence portfolio, we are focused on testing what works so that decisions about AI in development rest on rigorous evidence."

items.title: J-PALNew effort to advance AI in humanitarian emergencies launched at AidEx in Geneva 22 October 2026
items.summary:
GENEVA, SWITZERLAND – 22 OCTOBER 2026

A consortium of global humanitarian and development funders launched a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Humanitarian Working Group to help coordinate how AI can be used safely and effectively in humanitarian emergencies, Community Jameel announced today in Geneva, Switzerland, at the 2026 edition of AidEx, the world’s leading humanitarian aid and disaster relief event.

Jointly led by Community Jameel and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) in collaboration with the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) and the German development agency, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), the Working Group is part of the AI for Development (AI4D) Funders Collaborative, a global partnership of development funders dedicated to unite with partners around the world to centre challenges in the Global South and combat technological and social inequality by supporting inclusive, responsible AI made by and for communities.

Uzma Sulaiman, Associate Director of Community Jameel, announced the AI and Humanitarian Working Group during a panel at AidEx that brought together humanitarian organisations and funders, including FCDO, Enhancing Learning and Research for Humanitarian Assistance, Itad and NSDation Syria.

The new Working Group is launched as AI tools are increasingly being applied across humanitarian response, including in weather forecasting, rapid damage assessment, and other areas of technological innovation, while also raising risks around data privacy, surveillance, and the use of emerging technologies in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

The Working Group will provide a coordination role in assessing how AI is currently being used across the humanitarian sector, which will help to identify opportunities and risks and generate research and evidence to support policymakers and humanitarian organisations in the safe deployment of AI for conflict-affected populations. 

Uzma Sulaiman, Associate Director of Community Jameel, said: “Artificial intelligence has the potential to strengthen humanitarian response, from forecasting and early warning to assessing needs following crises. 

“At the same time, its use in fragile and conflict-affected settings raises important questions around safety, privacy, and accountability. 

“Through the new AI and Humanitarian Working Group, we want to help coordinate with key partners on the responsible use of AI for communities affected by conflict and crisis.”

This Working Group builds on other successes of the AI4D Funders Collaborative and the wider AI4D programme. In 2025, Community Jameel, FCDO, and IDRC launched a flagship AI4D initiative, the AI Evidence Alliance for Social Impact (AEASI), led by the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) and IDinsight, to evaluate and scale AI applications for social impact. 

AEASI is part of J-PAL’s wider evidence and AI portfolio, which also includes Project AI Evidence (PAIE), with USD 7 million from Community Jameel, IDRC, FCDO, Google.org, and Amazon Web Services, and the USD 60 million Evidence for AI in Health (EVAH) initiative, funded by Wellcome, the Gates Foundation, and the Novo Nordisk Foundation and delivered by J-PAL in partnership with the African Population and Health Research Center.

Mike Baily, Senior Advisor, AI, at J-PAL Global, said: "J-PAL welcomes efforts to build more evidence on how and where AI is improving people's livelihoods worldwide. items.content_html:
Perhaps more importantly, the elections offer contrasting tests of a similar model of political power. BiH's vote has largely reaffirmed the status quo, while Serbia's could overturn it. Both raise the question of how entrenched political elites have maintained their grip on power through patronage, institutional capture and unequal electoral competition, despite years of democratic stagnation. The question now is whether that formula is still working.

Preliminary results in BiH point to continuity rather than political realignment. The three parties that have dominated postwar politics - Party of Democratic Action (SDA) among predominantly Bosniak voters, Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) among Serb voters and Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) among Croat voters - once again emerged as the strongest forces. Although these three parties are likely to seek additional coalition partners, potentially including multiethnic parties, they will be able to form governments at all levels, diminishing the significance of any additional partners. Several parties that entered government after the 2022 elections lost considerable support, underscoring the lasting advantage of established party structures over newer, more personalized political projects.

The clearest winner, however, was Milorad Dodik. Although a 2025 conviction removed him from public office and barred him from political activity, the election demonstrated how little this weakened his control in Republika Srpska (RS), one of BiH’s two subnational entities under the constitutional framework established by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement. SNSD won the entity’s key races and remained its dominant political force, while a fragmented opposition failed to turn Dodik’s legal troubles into an electoral opening. Dodik’s son Igor is also increasingly mentioned publicly as a possible candidate for prime minister of RS, which would further consolidate the family’s control over the entity’s political life. Dodik now enters the post-election period without an official title but with renewed political leverage, including in his relationship with Belgrade.

Serbia's election represents the culmination of a political crisis that began with the Novi Sad railway station tragedy in November 2024, which killed 16 people. What began as student-led protests demanding accountability developed into the largest sustained protest movement of Vučić's fourteen-year rule, drawing support from citizens, political parties and civic organizations across Serbia. What makes this movement politically significant beyond Serbia is its ability to overcome a problem that has limited almost all recent protest movements globally: translating mass mobilization into an organized challenge for political power. Despite its leaderless, decentralized structure, it has sustained mobilization for almost two years, developed an electoral platform bringing together academics, professionals, famous sportsmen, activists and artists, and emerged as the principal challenger to an entrenched, authoritarian ruler. 

Recent polls and, perhaps more tellingly, the atmosphere on Serbia's streets suggest that an electoral breakthrough is a real possibility. The so-called Student List emerged as the principal challenger, with the prospect of securing enough seats to form a new government. Although eighteen electoral lists are competing, only a handful appear certain to cross the 3% parliamentary threshold, reinforcing the perception of a contest between two political alternatives. What was initially described as a referendum-like election has therefore taken on an almost plebiscitary character.

Vučić, meanwhile, has resigned the presidency and is campaigning as a private citizen, seeking to return to executive power as prime minister. Although no longer formally the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), he heads its electoral coalition, rebranded as “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia”. For the first time since 2012, he holds no public office. His possible electoral defeat could prolong that absence considerably, a prospect that might induce some separation anxiety in a leader so accustomed to exercising power with few checks.

Twenty-First-Century Technology, All Too Familiar Stale Politics

BiH’s election looked far more progressive than the politics it reproduced. For the first time nationwide, voters were authenticated electronically and ballots processed through optical scanners, measures imposed by the High Representative in March 2024 after domestic institutions failed to agree on electoral integrity reforms. Although observers reported problems with identification devices and scanner interruptions, they still assessed the process as a significant improvement. 

BiH used twenty-first-century technology to reproduce a 1990s political map, dominated by ethno-national parties and identity politics rather than reform or EU integration.

Turnout fell by nearly 10 percentage points compared with the previous elections, reaching a record low of around 42%. While this may reflect voter fatigue, stricter identification could also have reduced electoral fraud.  The official rate is also distorted by a voter register of roughly 3.4 million people in a country with an estimated resident population of fewer than three million. Members of the Central Election Commission have themselves called for a comprehensive review of the Central Voters’ Register. With about 1.4 million ballots cast, the low official turnout may therefore reflect not only abstention but also a cleaner electoral process and an inflated register. 

Yet electoral technologies can improve the integrity of election day without addressing the many irregularities that occur before and during the campaign. Civil society observers documented numerous abuses in this cycle, including the misuse of public resources through intensified public works and campaigning by public officials, one-off payments to vulnerable groups and the use of children in campaign activities. In most cases, the Central Election Commission did not sanction the violations on the grounds on which they had been reported, while the penalties imposed have mainly concerned premature campaigning and have been too low to have a meaningful deterrent effect. 

Media coverage was particularly skewed in RS, where the public broadcaster overwhelmingly favored the ruling SNSD. According to Transparency International in BiH, SNSD received 28 hours of airtime, compared with just minutes for the opposition. The imbalance was especially stark in the RS presidential race: the SNSD candidate received over five hours of coverage, against just 69 seconds for his opponent.

Old Tricks, a New Challenger

Meanwhile, Serbia approaches its election with more traditional technology but all too familiar integrity problems. Serbian election watchdog organization, CRTA, is conducting long-term observation and has documented pressure on voters, misuse of public resources and extreme media inequality. The increasingly confrontational campaign has also raised fears of further violence, with election observers and civil society actors warning that political tensions could escalate before or after polling day. The local elections that took place in spring 2026 were already marked by intimidation and violence.

The comprehensive audit of the Unified Voter Register, repeatedly recommended by ODIHR, will not be completed before the election. To illustrate the scale of the problem with the Register, Serbia has close to 6.5 million registered voters, nearly as many as its entire 2022 census population, children included.

Traditional media, largely captured by the regime, are flooded with political propaganda in favor of the ruling party. 

During just one monitored week in September, representatives of the ruling majority received three-quarters of television airtime allocated to political actors, while CRTA documented more than 1,200 public activities by senior state officials in the preceding months. CRTA also estimates that the announced pre-election one-off payment measures amount to almost €1 billion, raising concerns about the use of public money for electoral advantage.  

Disputed voter registrations and reported obstacles to voting abroad add to concerns about an exceptionally unequal electoral contest. This time, more than 100,000 members of the Serbian diaspora have registered to vote abroad, roughly three times as many as in previous elections. Many are deeply dissatisfied with Vučić's rule, which, for some, was among the reasons they left Serbia in the first place. Yet polling stations remain unavailable in some countries with substantial demand, while many new spots have opened in RS. In Germany, Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs officials even claimed they had requested additional polling stations, only for the German Embassy in Belgrade to confirm that no such request had been received. 

There is also a literal connection between the integrity of Serbia's election and that of BiH: the voters themselves. Serbia's disputed 2023 election exposed organized voter migration from RS, including questionable residency registrations used to bolster the ruling party's majorities in targeted municipalities. While voting by dual citizens is a legitimate democratic right, manipulating residence registration or using state resources to engineer electoral advantage in this manner is another matter. 

However, this time something new happened. The Student List campaigned directly among Serbian citizens in several cities in RS and Brčko District, where Serbian opposition actors have had little presence. The campaign faced police interventions and incidents occurred before it was suspended for safety reasons. Yet these institutional pressures did not produce broader solidarity among political parties or student organizations in RS. Some student groups close to the ruling SNSD publicly opposed the Student List, while support came mainly from individual opposition politicians and parts of civil society. This limited response also reflected the cautious calculations of RS opposition parties toward developments in Serbia. Some of these parties have at times depended on political and financial support from Serbia’s governing structures. More broadly, mainstream RS parties place ties with Serbia, viewed as the Serb national homeland, at the centre of their ethno-national agendas and therefore rarely criticize Belgrade’s domestic politics or policies toward BiH and RS. Even so, an electorate long approached almost exclusively through the SNS–SNSD relationship has become contested political territory.

After 25 October: Who Holds Power?

BiH's elections have reinforced the status quo, with Dodik retaining political influence despite losing office. Serbia's election, meanwhile, could either consolidate Vučić's rule or end fourteen years of SNS rule, potentially reshaping the Vučić–Dodik alliance and relations between Belgrade and Banja Luka, and, consequently, between Belgrade and Sarajevo. Two scenarios illustrate what is at stake on both sides of the Drina.

The first is continuity. If SNS retains power, Vučić's return as prime minister would preserve a political system built around a single dominant authoritarian leader. Given the escalation of repression and institutional pressure over the past two years, further democratic decline would be expected. Serbia could move toward the more openly repressive political models seen in Georgia or Belarus, although these remain warnings rather than inevitable outcomes. Serbia's relations with BiH would likely continue to be seen through the prism of the Vučić–Dodik alliance and would also depend on which political party controlled BiH's foreign-affairs portfolio. 

During Vučić's rule, Belgrade has largely bypassed Sarajevo, focusing instead on the special relations between Serbia and RS and on the alliance's formal and informal networks. In Sarajevo, this approach has often been seen as enabling activities detrimental to BiH's constitutional order and sovereignty.

The second scenario is a Student List victory and Serbia's first national transfer of power since 2012. But winning an election and taking control of a captured state are two different things. Vučić is no longer the formal SNS president, yet he could retain considerable influence through party structures and networks of political loyalty and influence built over fourteen years in power. The approaching presidential election, which must take place before the end of the year, adds another complication. A student-backed parliamentary majority could coexist with an SNS-backed president, creating competing centres of political authority. Even if SNS lost both elections, Vučić could remain an influential figure outside government, although his ability to exercise power would depend on whether those networks survived the loss of office. Most importantly, SNS would retain control of most towns and municipalities across Serbia. Although much of this local power structure depends on access to central government resources and could weaken without them, it would not disappear overnight, leaving Vučić with a considerable political foothold outside national office.

Dodik's position in RS offers an interesting parallel. Both leaders could find themselves outside public office while remaining politically influential, though under different circumstances. This could complicate relations across the Drina. A new Serbian government would have little reason to abandon its institutional ties with RS, which extend well beyond the two leaders. The students' campaign there already suggests that they intend to challenge SNS's political monopoly rather than Serbia's relationship with Banja Luka. This continuity helps explain the region’s skepticism toward potential political change in Serbia: a shift in electoral power in Belgrade would not necessarily change Serbia's regional relationships or, at least, its approach to BiH. Even in the event of a change in power, Dodik might continue to treat Vučić as his principal political ally, even if someone else were running Serbia. Belgrade and Banja Luka could then have a relationship running on two parallel tracks.

Can Political Turnover Restart European Integration?

Electoral continuity also leaves the institutional obstacles that have stalled BiH’s European integration largely unchanged. The EU was almost entirely absent as a campaign issue, while parties formally committed to membership rarely turned that commitment into concrete reform proposals. SNSD went further by portraying EU demands on the rule of law and institutional reform as measures directed against RS and the Serb population. 

The consequences of this stagnation are increasingly clear. More than two years after the European Council agreed to open accession negotiations in March 2024, the conditions for moving forward have been progressively scaled back in the hope of securing at least a minimal political consensus, yet even that has proved impossible. BiH also remains the regional laggard in accessing the Reform and Growth Facility. Delays have already resulted in the loss of 10% of its allocation, while the country still lacks access to nearly EUR 1 billion of its allocated funds. 

As Brussels has struggled to build domestic momentum, political actors have increasingly turned to other centres of power. Dodik best illustrates this shift. His ties with Moscow remain strong, as shown by his meeting with Vladimir Putin days before the election, while the Trump administration’s decision to lift sanctions imposed on him and his associates for actions that undermined the Dayton Peace Agreement and for systemic corruption marked a major shift in Washington’s approach. Dodik has actively used RS’s lobbying networks in the US and cast both Trump and Putin as key to his political recovery. While the EU ties financial support and accession progress to institutional reform, other external actors offer political access, investment, or security ties without the same conditionalities. For political elites used to avoiding hard domestic compromises, such alternatives may seem increasingly attractive. With the parties behind much of the previous mandate’s deadlock still central to government formation, and record-low turnout showing growing distance between citizens and politics, the election results offer little reason to expect rapid change.

For Serbia, the two scenarios imply completely different trajectories. An SNS victory would preserve the existing relationship with Brussels: formal commitment to EU membership alongside continued deterioration in democratic standards. A Student List victory could restart the accession process through institutional reform and anti-corruption measures, although Kosovo and other foreign-policy disagreements would likely remain major political issues that are difficult to resolve.

Political change could also make Serbia a less predictable EU partner. The student movement has criticized Brussels' tolerance of Vučić's democratic backsliding, and a new government might prove less accommodating on several issues. This exposes a contradiction in the EU's approach to the Western Balkans. For years, Brussels has been criticized for prioritizing predictable leaders over democratic standards. A transfer of power could initially create greater uncertainty, particularly if Vučić retained influence outside government or the presidency became a centre of political contestation in the near future.

The EU would then face a choice between the predictability of established political relationships and the uncertainties of democratic change. After years of being accused of trading democracy for stability, Brussels may have to accept some instability to get democracy back on track. Without meaningful democratic progress, its ambitious enlargement goals in the Western Balkans are unlikely to be achieved.

A Student List victory could restart the accession process through institutional reform and anti-corruption measures, although Kosovo and other foreign-policy disagreements would likely remain major political issues that are difficult to resolve.

Political change could also make Serbia a less predictable EU partner. The student movement has criticized Brussels' tolerance of Vučić's democratic backsliding, and a new government might prove less accommodating on several issues. This exposes a contradiction in the EU's approach to the Western Balkans. For years, Brussels has been criticized for prioritizing predictable leaders over democratic standards. A transfer of power could initially create greater uncertainty, particularly if Vučić retained influence outside government or the presidency became a centre of political contestation in the near future.

The EU would then face a choice between the predictability of established political relationships and the uncertainties of democratic change. After years of being accused of trading democracy for stability, Brussels may have to accept some instability to get democracy back on track. Without meaningful democratic progress, its ambitious enlargement goals in the Western Balkans are unlikely to be achieved.

When I read the news that Navi Pillay had been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, I felt something that has become increasingly difficult to sustain in today’s political climate: a renewed sense of hope. And with it, an unwavering determination to keep striving for a world built on the equal worth of every human being.

Yet on the very day that a lifetime dedicated to defending international law and universal human rights was being honoured, one of the institutions entrusted with upholding those principles was facing renewed political pressure. That same day, the United States formally announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court, where Pillay once served as a judge. Although the measures had long been in preparation, the coincidence of their announcement with her Nobel recognition could hardly have been more striking.

That Pillay is South African makes this moment even more poignant. South Africa’s decision to bring proceedings against Israel before the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention has itself become a source of diplomatic tension and pressure.

The convergence is deeply revealing. A South African woman is honoured for a lifetime devoted to international justice, while an international court faces sanctions and her own country confronts diplomatic pressure for invoking international law. Together, these developments expose a fundamental contradiction in today’s international order: the gap between the universal principles of international law and the geopolitical interests that influence how, when and against whom they are upheld.

Pillay’s personal journey is equally moving. A woman who grew up under apartheid, in a country where the law itself was an instrument of racial oppression, went on to become one of the world’s leading defenders of international law and universal human rights.

For me, her recognition evokes the extraordinary promise of South Africa’s democratic struggle: the belief that injustice can be confronted, that entrenched systems of oppression can be transformed, and that freedom carries responsibilities extending far beyond national borders.

It also reminds me why the struggle for democracy was never simply about who governs. It was, and remains, about the kind of society we believe every human being deserves to live in.

This is why I see this Nobel Peace Prize as both an immense source of hope and a powerful call to action. Not out of nostalgia for a more hopeful past, but out of the conviction that the ideals which have guided our struggles for justice, democracy and peace remain as relevant and necessary as ever. The frustrations of the present should not narrow our vision of what is possible or weaken our determination to pursue it.

A South African legacy that belongs to the world

The Nobel Peace Prize has always carried political significance, even when recognising achievements that transcend partisan politics. Despite its own controversies, it retains an extraordinary capacity to draw global attention to individuals and principles whose importance extends beyond the calculations of governments. It remains a distinction coveted by some of the world’s most powerful political leaders. South Africa has a remarkable history with the Nobel Peace Prize. Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk were recognised, in different circumstances, for their contributions to overcoming apartheid and advancing peaceful political transformation.

Navi Pillay adds another chapter to that history, representing a remarkable journey from resistance against an oppressive national political order to the defence of a universal international legal order. 

From defending anti-apartheid activists to serving at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the International Criminal Court and as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Pillay has devoted her career to advancing justice beyond the boundaries of nationality, political power and privilege.

At the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, her work helped establish landmark jurisprudence recognising that sexual violence, including rape, can constitute genocide, bringing violence disproportionately experienced by women into the international pursuit of justice and accountability.

Pillay’s commitment to justice speaks to the deeper significance of South Africa’s liberation struggle. It was more than a rejection of apartheid. At its most visionary, it affirmed the universality of human dignity and the conviction that no political system should determine whose humanity counts and whose does not. That conviction inspired international solidarity and demonstrated how a struggle for freedom in one country could resonate across the world.

Pillay embodies this internationalist legacy. Her recognition is a moment of national pride. But beyond that, it reminds us that some of South Africa’s most important contributions to the world have come from those who understood that freedom and justice cannot be confined within national borders.

When defending international law comes at a political cost

Pillay’s career gives this question a particular urgency.

Her leadership of the United Nations Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory places her at the centre of debates over accountability and the uneven application of international law.

For a country whose liberation struggle was sustained by international solidarity and the rejection of institutionalised injustice, this commitment is inseparable from its democratic legacy. Honouring that legacy requires South Africa to defend universal rights consistently, including when violations are committed by political partners, allies or governments with which it maintains important strategic relationships. Its credibility rests not only on the principles it invokes, but on its willingness to uphold them even when doing so comes at a political cost.

Against this backdrop, the Nobel Peace Prize affirms something fundamental: law must constrain power, accountability must be universal, and the protection of human dignity cannot depend on the nationality of victims, the identity of perpetrators or the geopolitical interests of their allies.

The Nobel Prize in a World Where Might Increasingly Prevails over Right

In recognising Navi Pillay, the Nobel Committee has made an important intervention in the debate about the future of global governance at a time of profound transformation of the international order.

Multilateral institutions face growing challenges to their legitimacy and authority, while major powers increasingly resort to unilateral action, coercive diplomacy and geopolitical bargaining. International law itself risks becoming subordinate to the interests of the powerful rather than serving as a universal framework for constraining their power.

Yet the credibility of the international system has also long been undermined by its own contradictions. For much of the Global South, promises of universal rights and sovereign equality have coexisted with colonial legacies, unequal economic structures, selective accountability and the concentration of decision-making power in a handful of states.

Simply preserving the international order as it exists will not resolve these contradictions. We must defend and transform it so that its universal principles become genuinely universal in practice.

This requires confronting historical inequalities, challenging double standards, strengthening accountability and ensuring that countries and societies historically excluded from global decision-making can meaningfully shape the rules governing our collective future.

Pillay's career is compelling proof that international institutions, however imperfect, can be instruments through which power is challenged, rights are defended and justice becomes possible. Her Nobel Peace Prize, and its global resonance, offer a powerful affirmation that the pursuit of a more just, inclusive and genuinely universal international order is both possible and urgently necessary.

A reason for hope, and a responsibility to act

At a time when wars, democratic erosion and the rise of exclusionary and authoritarian politics make it increasingly difficult to remain optimistic about the direction of global affairs, it is easy to become disillusioned and to question whether the values that have inspired generations of struggles for justice, democracy and peace still have the power to shape our future.

Yet there are moments when the defence of these principles is not merely acknowledged but celebrated.

Pillay's life's work is a powerful reminder that even deeply entrenched systems of oppression can be challenged and transformed, and that the political realities of today are neither inevitable nor irreversible.

The values we believe in have not become obsolete simply because they are under attack. On the contrary, the current political moment makes their defence more urgent than ever.

For me, this recognition is therefore both a profound source of hope and a call to action: to resist disillusionment and resignation, to confront injustice consistently, and to strengthen the solidarity and collective action needed to uphold the ideals we strive for.

It reminds us that hope is not a passive expectation of a better future, but a conviction that change remains possible and a commitment to making it happen.

This article first appeared here: za.boell.org

For intersex people and their concerns, 2015 was a very important year because it saw intersex issues being thrust more and more into the spotlight of European and international policy making. Caroline Ausserer talks about these developments with Dan Christian Ghattas, co-chair of OII Europe, the umbrella organization of European human rights-based intersex NGOs.

Caroline Ausserer: The year 2015 saw intersex issues figure more prominently on the political agenda, bringing in its wake a shift in attitudes. Looking back at the events of the past year, what would you say the high points were?   

Dan Christian Ghattas: The most important high point was the new law passed in Malta in April 2015, the Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act. It is the first law in the world that makes it a punishable offense to carry out medical and surgical interventions on intersex minors without informed consent provided that these interventions – because they do not constitute life-saving procedures – can be deferred. We underlined the significance of this law in our press release, and I recently had the opportunity to once again point out the importance of this law for Germany at a symposium hosted by the German Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth (BMFSFJ). But a number of other very important things also happened in 2015. OII Germany, for example, organized a thematic briefing for the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) as part of its Universal Periodic Review of Germany and also gave the Committee an introduction to the topic of intersex. We were very pleased that the Committee in its concluding observations called on the German government to finally take the measures outlined in the recommendations made by the Committee against Torture (CAT) concerning the protection of the human rights of intersex people in Germany. OII Europe subsequently drafted a statement on intersex and disability that was very well-received internationally. Germany is now called upon to implement the UN’s recommendations. Another high point was the publication in May of two major documents that were presented to the public at the IDAHO Forum in Montenegro: an issue paper of the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights and an initial study on the legal situation of intersex people by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA).  

What is the significance of these studies?

The issue paper “Human rights and intersex people” published by the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights – to which OII Europe and national intersex NGOs contributed in an advisory capacity – outlines the current state of affairs, identifies obstacles to the enjoyment of human rights, discloses rights violations, and offers recommendations that states should take to heart. The study “The fundamental rights situation of intersex people,” conducted by the Agency for Fundamental Rights, examines the situation of intersex people from a civil status perspective and investigates their inclusion in anti-discrimination legislation. The findings, in a nutshell, are sobering. The FRA also looks into an enormously important issue – the actual number of interventions. Among other conclusions, it finds that it is practically impossible in Europe to obtain statistical data on the subject, particularly data on medical interventions. NGOs have been making precisely this complaint for years, and I also aired this grievance in the study “Human Rights between the Sexes – A preliminary study on the life situations of inter* individuals,” which I did for the Heinrich Böll Foundation in 2013. Now, it has finally been officially verified by an EU agency.        

In Strasbourg in September, both papers were presented again at a seminar event in which OII Europe took part. Parallel to this second presentation, we had very fruitful meetings with decision makers from the European Parliament and the Council of Europe and noticed a growing awareness that, first of all, intersex people exist, and second, that unconsented interventions on intersex people are being seen more and more as a human rights issue. Support for the view that intersex is solely a medical issue is increasingly diminishing. The Maltese law, the issue paper of the Commissioner for Human Rights, and the FRA study are the yardsticks against which future governments must measure themselves.          

What were some other notable events in 2015?

A UN expert meeting on intersex and human rights was held in September. I was invited as a representative of OII Europe as were other intersex experts from five continents. Its aim was to inform UN experts about the situation of intersex people around the world. Following the meeting we intersex experts hosted a public side event on the human rights of intersex people as part of the 30th session of the UN Human Rights Council. It is important to mention that the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights highlighted the situation of intersex people in his opening remarks for this very session and also opened the expert meeting. This sends a wonderful signal that human rights violations against intersex people have moved to the center of human rights discourse. Another high point in Europe was the second European Intersex Meeting, which was held in Athens in late October prior to ILGA-Europe’s annual conference. In November, a further highlight took place in Germany, namely, the BMFSFJ’s symposium on consultation support for intersex people and their family members. Plus, I just returned from an Inter* Conference in Vienna. 

There is a lot happening everywhere: at the international, European, and national levels. The developments at the international and European level ripple back to the countries while the experiences of the individual countries find their way into European and international advocacy work. This dynamic is very important.

OII Europe recently became a non-profit NGO. How did this come about?

OII Europe was founded as the European network of national OIIs on Human Rights Day, December 10, during the 2012 ILGA World Conference in Stockholm. Individual national NGOs, including OII Germany, had been working intensively on the issue since 2009, and we wanted to connect our efforts. This year, on September 25, 2015, we registered OII Europe here in Berlin as a non-profit association under German law.

How do you work and how is OII Europe financed?

Since 2009, when we began working at the European level, we have received support from ILGA-Europe, which TGEU put us into contact with. All of this would not have been possible without ILGA-Europe’s contacts, networks, and travel grants. We all continue to work on a volunteer basis and are pushing our health to the limit. In 2015, the US-based Astraea Lesbian Foundation for Justice established the Intersex Human Rights Fund. This fund support 29 projects around the world with a total of 187,000 US dollars; the maximum amount of funding per project is 10,000 US dollars. We at OII Europe receive support for our web project European Intersex Visibility Works, but this, of course, does not cover staff costs or the costs that arise from our political advocacy work. The project is extremely important to us because it addresses one of the challenges that we constantly face in Europe: the multiplicity of languages and the lack of depathologizing information on intersexuality in many languages. The web platform will include audio and video clips from intersex people as well as translations of important human rights texts on intersex. The aim is to create a platform that enables people, no matter where they are, to inform themselves about intersexuality from a human rights perspective. The platform is slated to go online next year.

What are the possible dangers if OII Europe continues to lack funding?

Our personal lives, our financial security and our health have so far taken a back seat to our work as activists. That we receive funding – OII Europe as well as the national intersex NGOs – is a major wish of us all, because without funding it will be impossible to carry out our projects and to continue our work. Working without a solid financial basis poses huge health risks. Many intersex people are still living under a cloak of invisibility, and building networks is a lengthy process. Since intersex people continue to be subjected to discrimination after “coming out,” deciding to be publicly visible is a very conscious choice. Because once you have started, there is no turning back, and it can have negative consequences such as losing your job, which has recently happened again. It is still a big taboo. What’s more, going public requires a whole other step: the first step is to recognize one’s own internalized pathologization and to free oneself from it. That is not an easy thing to do. Although the movement is constantly growing, there are lots of barriers, including some related to interventions, that prevent many people from joining in.

What are the priorities for 2016?

We will continue to pursue the possibilities that opened up in 2015. This means continuing our work at the EU, Council of Europe, and UN levels. Another priority is, as already mentioned, the search for funding. We also plan to get in touch with other groups that are subject to similar human rights violations. So far we have cooperated mainly with LGBTI organizations. If our resources permit us to do so, we want to establish closer ties in 2016 with the deaf community, whose members face a very similar pathologization. Initial talks already took place in 2013 and 2014 at the Douarnenez Film Festival, which focuses on cultural minorities and is held in France’s Breton region. The festival has been in close contact with OII Francophonie for several years and has now made intersex a major emphasis in its program. The deaf community has also been active there for several years, for example, with the program The World of Deaf People.

If you had one wish, what would it be?

I wish to see a global society in which the existence of more than two biological genders and identities is celebrated. That way, unconsented interventions would no longer be an issue and thus an absolute no-go. At the same time, it must be made clear that even when we put an end to the interventions, a large part of the discrimination against intersex people will remain as long as they are perceived to be ill or genderless or “freaks.” Our goal must be to create a society in which the existence of intersex people is just as common and natural as that of blue-eyed people.

Thank you for talking with me.

In November, a further highlight took place in Germany, namely, the BMFSFJ’s symposium on consultation support for intersex people and their family members. Plus, I just returned from an Inter* Conference in Vienna. 

There is a lot happening everywhere: at the international, European, and national levels. The developments at the international and European level ripple back to the countries while the experiences of the individual countries find their way into European and international advocacy work. This dynamic is very important.

OII Europe recently became a non-profit NGO. How did this come about?

OII Europe was founded as the European network of national OIIs on Human Rights Day, December 10, during the 2012 ILGA World Conference in Stockholm. Individual national NGOs, including OII Germany, had been working intensively on the issue since 2009, and we wanted to connect our efforts. This year, on September 25, 2015, we registered OII Europe here in Berlin as a non-profit association under German law.

How do you work and how is OII Europe financed?

Since 2009, when we began working at the European level, we have received support from ILGA-Europe, which TGEU put us into contact with. All of this would not have been possible without ILGA-Europe’s contacts, networks, and travel grants. We all continue to work on a volunteer basis and are pushing our health to the limit. In 2015, the US-based Astraea Lesbian Foundation for Justice established the Intersex Human Rights Fund. This fund support 29 projects around the world with a total of 187,000 US dollars; the maximum amount of funding per project is 10,000 US dollars. We at OII Europe receive support for our web project European Intersex Visibility Works, but this, of course, does not cover staff costs or the costs that arise from our political advocacy work. The project is extremely important to us because it addresses one of the challenges that we constantly face in Europe: the multiplicity of languages and the lack of depathologizing information on intersexuality in many languages. The web platform will include audio and video clips from intersex people as well as translations of important human rights texts on intersex. The aim is to create a platform that enables people, no matter where they are, to inform themselves about intersexuality from a human rights perspective. The platform is slated to go online next year.

What are the possible dangers if OII Europe continues to lack funding?

Our personal lives, our financial security and our health have so far taken a back seat to our work as activists. That we receive funding – OII Europe as well as the national intersex NGOs – is a major wish of us all, because without funding it will be impossible to carry out our projects and to continue our work. Working without a solid financial basis poses huge health risks. Many intersex people are still living under a cloak of invisibility, and building networks is a lengthy process. Since intersex people continue to be subjected to discrimination after “coming out,” deciding to be publicly visible is a very conscious choice. Because once you have started, there is no turning back, and it can have negative consequences such as losing your job, which has recently happened again. It is still a big taboo. What’s more, going public requires a whole other step: the first step is to recognize one’s own internalized pathologization and to free oneself from it. That is not an easy thing to do. Although the movement is constantly growing, there are lots of barriers, including some related to interventions, that prevent many people from joining in.

What are the priorities for 2016?

We will continue to pursue the possibilities that opened up in 2015. This means continuing our work at the EU, Council of Europe, and UN levels. Another priority is, as already mentioned, the search for funding. We also plan to get in touch with other groups that are subject to similar human rights violations. So far we have cooperated mainly with LGBTI organizations. If our resources permit us to do so, we want to establish closer ties in 2016 with the deaf community, whose members face a very similar pathologization. Initial talks already took place in 2013 and 2014 at the Douarnenez Film Festival, which focuses on cultural minorities and is held in France’s Breton region. The festival has been in close contact with OII Francophonie for several years and has now made intersex a major emphasis in its program. The deaf community has also been active there for several years, for example, with the program The World of Deaf People.

If you had one wish, what would it be?

I wish to see a global society in which the existence of more than two biological genders and identities is celebrated. That way, unconsented interventions would no longer be an issue and thus an absolute no-go. At the same time, it must be made clear that even when we put an end to the interventions, a large part of the discrimination against intersex people will remain as long as they are perceived to be ill or genderless or “freaks.” Our goal must be to create a society in which the existence of intersex people is just as common and natural as that of blue-eyed people.

Thank you for talking with me.

Lena Herrmann-Green is a 19-year-old student with two younger siblings who lives a relatively normal life. But she was one of the first children in Germany to be conceived via anonymous sperm donation.

“People are always asking me if I miss my father and want to meet him,” says Lena Herrmann-Green with a self-assurance that comes from years of media experience. She collaborated on a book on the topic at the age of nine, recently spoke before the European Parliament, and was one of the main speakers at the Rainbow Families Meeting that took place outside Lisbon in October 2015. “I have a problem with the definition of ‘father,’ because for me that is someone who loves you and is there for you,” explains Lena. “In this sense I don’t have a father but rather two parents who love me, and I don’t need anyone else. We are complete as we are; there is nothing missing.” She adds that constant questions about a father show the extent to which people disqualify family models that don’t fit the traditional father-mother-child mold, stressing that it is finally time to put an end to this. After a moment of pause, Lena tosses back her hair and rolls her eyes and says: “I'm the product of artificial insemination and I don’t have three eyes.”

As a kid, she says, she relished the attention given to her family and enjoyed discussing her experience. “Back then I openly told everyone of my background, but my family situation did not affect how I lived my daily life,” reports Lena. One of her mothers is Dr. Lisa Green. The dedicated psychotherapist and co-founder of NELFA, the Network of European LGBTI Families Associations, clearly understands that children in rainbow families perceive their families as “normal,” and that they must first grasp why the outside world shows interest in them. As she sees it, they must first, so to speak, be initiated into heterosexual society. In workshops titled “Strong Parents Strengthen Children – Preparing the Path to Heterosexual Society,” Dr. Green sheds light on this topic and shares her experiences as a lesbian mother. It becomes clear where Lena got her confidence from. “Our parents walked us through a whole bunch of questions, and also used role-playing exercises to prepare us for possible reactions to our family,” she says.   

Lena’s parents separated when she was 13, which made her withdraw from the world and not want to give any more interviews. “The problem was the constant need to prove that there was nothing wrong with our family, says Lena. “I no longer had any desire to explain my situation and to demonstrate how great my family is.” She describes how parents and children in rainbow families are under enormous pressure to be role models and to not make any mistakes. “The pressure to be perfect comes from outside and from within, but that doesn’t mean that rainbow parents expect their kids to be perfect,” explains Lena. “It rather means that we belong to a minority that is not yet fully accepted. Because so many changes are occurring in the political arena regarding this issue, every statement I make can have a significant impact.” It becomes clear that this issue is now her main priority, and that the awareness of the responsibility weighs heavily on her. This makes her chief concern even more understandable. “The pressure must be taken away!” she says. “Rainbow families must finally be allowed to make mistakes.”



 Lena sees the recognition of rainbow families as families under the law as the first step toward easing some of this pressure: "I hope that the view spreads that recognizing our families as families should be a matter of course, and that this relieves the pressure of having to prove oneself."

So far, only a fourth of Europe’s countries have recognized rainbow families. The result is that large numbers of such families live in a no-man’s land fraught with discriminatory practices, which particularly cause the children to suffer. Not allowing the recognition of both parents as legal guardians – through, for example, the granting of full adoption rights, i.e. joint adoption and second-parent adoption – is tantamount to not recognizing the family as such. Second-parent adoption puts stepchildren on the same legal footing as biological children. Until 2005, when second-parent adoption became possible in Germany, only one parent was legally registered as such in Lena’s family; the other mother was “a nobody in the eyes of the law.”

Today, 13 of 47 European countries grant full adoption rights. This includes Andorra (2014), Belgium (2006), Denmark (2010), France (2013), Iceland (2006), Ireland (soon), Luxembourg (2014), Malta (2014), the Netherlands (2001), Norway (2009), Spain (2005), Sweden (2003), and the United Kingdom (2005/2013). Three of 47 allow second-parent adoption: Austria (2013), Germany (2014), and Slovenia (2011). Starting in 2016, Austria will permit full adoption and Estonia second-parent adoption. In November 2015, Portugal’s parliament voiced its support for extending adoption rights to same-sex couples.

Lena Herrmann-Green wishes to see a Europe in which no legal distinctions are made between same-sex and other-sex parents and in which family diversity is considered an enrichment and treated as such in practice. “After all, the family is where there is love,” she points out, “no matter what the parents’ genders are.” As a spokesperson for family diversity, that is something she will surely have to repeat frequently.

With a backlog of more than 350,000 asylum applications, Germany is under pressure to speed up the asylum process. But efforts to quickly process Syrian refugees have resulted in asylum decisions on the basis of nationality rather than case-by-case. That’s good for Syrians, but it shortchanges Afghanis and others fleeing violence and conflict.

An Afghan doctor wearing a tracksuit stands on the muddy ground inside a temporary registration shelter for asylum-seekers in the western German state of Baden-Württemberg, waving a paper flyer announcing German classes. “Why not us?” he asks.

The full-time class was being offered to Syrians, Iraqis, Eritreans, and Iranians, but Afghans and other nationalities were not mentioned. The discrepancy points to a new multi-tiered approach in how Germany is processing asylum-seekers—one based at least initially on national origin.

In a particularly chaotic year for migration to Europe, Afghans represent the second largest group of migrants traversing the Mediterranean Sea, after Syrians. But though their country is riven by fighting with the Taliban and other armed groups, they have received a different welcome. Instead of fast-tracked applications and pledges to make integration a top priority, Germany is labeling them as economic migrants and telling them to stay home.

To read the rest of this article in Quartz click here. Research was supported by the Transatlantic Media Fellowship Program.

Towards a Locally-led Peacebuilding (LLPB) self-assessment tool

To move the ‘localisation’ agenda into concrete action with and beyond their partners a small steering group (SG) of funding institutions (PeaceNexus Foundation, Robert Bosch Stiftung, Humanity United and the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs) initiated a process to develop a tool to self-assess and advance the quality of locally-led practice.

The tool is adapted to the peacebuilding sector, with a strong emphasis on conflict sensitivity and context-driven role allocation in settings that are increasingly restricted. It also puts locally-led principles into practice by ensuring that changes in practice are informed by input from partners and reflected in partnership agreements.

The tool aims to:

  • assist INGOs, networks or other re-granters to take stock of their own performance and be a guide to self-assessment and internal change in line with locally-led principles;
  • inform conversations with local and international actors, to advance equitable partnership practices.

A first version of the tool was developed with other funders, intermediaries and local partners in a workshop in The Hague in April 2025 and has been tested by participants of the workshop since then.

All partners used portions of the tool that were most relevant to them, adapting and integrating into their processes in different ways: the questions were used in surveys for staff and partners and in facilitated discussions. Conversation about purpose, language and safety were held, but there were nevertheless challenges in enabling honest critical feedback from partners.

Testing is still on-going and the group re-convened in September to review experience and results. International Alert, Search for Common Ground, Peace Direct, WANEP, Resolve Network , GPPAC, and others found that the tool created structured space for difficult conversations, encouraged teams to reflect on partnership practices and identify specific internal processes or gaps to be addressed.

In these review meetings, it was also agreed to share the framework and questions used as-is, with a clear caveat that it is a working version. The invitation is therefore to take what is useful, adapt it, simplify it and integrate it in existing organisational processes.

The intention of the Steering Group is to share it via peer-learning spaces and donor roundtables, to contribute to existing conversations, including those around implementing the new Practical Guidelines for Supporting Locally Led Development | OECD and the Call-to-Action that followed its publication.

Please contact carole.frampton@peacenexus.org if you have any questions or plan to use the tool. Our hope is that this initiative will help change both partnering and funding modalities, as well as encourage more donors to select intermediaries that walk the talk of locally-led peacebuilding.

Downloadable links:

    • Locally-led Peacebuilding Assessment tool
    • Tool Guidance Note

COP17 will mark the first global review of collective progress toward implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), adopted in 2022 as the strategic plan for implementing the CBD through 2030.

The global review’s final outcome will be negotiated at COP17. It is based largely on CBD Parties’ national reports and the global report on collective progress in implementing the goals and targets of the GBF. The latter, entitled State of Biodiversity Action, will be released before COP17, but the draft already highlights the slow pace of progress.

Implementation not on track

The focus of the global review is therefore mainly on the inadequate implementation of the GBF – the “implementation gap”. This includes developed countries’ fulfillment of their obligations to provide the means of implementation – finance, technology transfer, and capacity building – to developing countries. Most of the world’s biodiversity lies in developing countries, so they bear the greater burden of implementation. They are reluctant to increase these burdens and introduce new ones related to planning, monitoring, reporting and review when developed countries are not meeting their obligations to provide the means of implementation. 

These are important issues; however, without addressing the underlying causes driving biodiversity destruction, it will not be possible to meet the GBF’s goals and targets. The root causes include the rules of the economic and financial system that drive extractivism at the expense of social and environmental well-being, financial flows that fund sectors driving biodiversity loss, regulatory capture by corporations, and the flaws of market logic applied to biodiversity. These causes are rooted in inequitable systems of exploitation and control and create a “justice gap”, which must be seriously confronted.

Biodiversity finance debates

The discussions at COP17 will also center on the “finance gap”, which is usually understood as a shortfall in the financing needed to tackle the biodiversity crisis. Addressing this gap is framed as mobilizing resources from “all sources”.

In fact, the CBD places equity at the center of biodiversity finance. While all Parties have obligations to implement the Convention, there are differentiated obligations for the provision of financial resources. The extent to which developing countries effectively implement their obligations will depend on how well developed countries fulfill their legally binding obligations to provide new and additional financial resources and transfer technology. Article 20 articulates the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR). 
 
But these financing obligations have yet to be met, with funding amounts falling far short of the GBF’s targets. Instead, at COP17, the political fight will focus on “broadening the contributor base”. Proposals from developed countries for sovereign contributions to be automatically triggered based on income levels can be viewed as an attempt to undermine CBDR and Article 20 and to avoid their obligations to provide financial resources.

The emphasis on mobilizing resources from “all sources” again sidesteps developed countries’ obligations to provide finance and instead looks to the private sector and “innovative schemes”, such as biodiversity offsets and credits, to fill the “finance gap”. In practice, however, these schemes fail to generate the necessary finance and often deepen social and ecological harm.

Another key area of contention is the criteria for the institutional structure that will operate the CBD’s financial mechanism. Developing countries have long called for a global biodiversity fund under the authority of the COP – one that can build momentum and raise ambition for greater financial resources and that has equitable governance arrangements.

Getting the criteria right, including how Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth can obtain direct financing and participate in governance, will be important in ensuring that the institutional structure operates equitably and justly.

Ensuring climate priorities don’t undermine biodiversity and human rights

A key overarching issue at COP17 will be the integration of biodiversity and climate action and how to translate this into coherent national policies and implementation. A related issue is cooperation among the three Rio Conventions: the CBD, UNFCCC and UNCCD. COP17 will consider options for greater policy coherence and a potential long-term roadmap for cooperation. The challenge is ensuring that biodiversity remains the primary concern of the CBD and that synergies respect distinct mandates without subordinating biodiversity action to carbon-related priorities.

COP17 will also consider a supplement to the voluntary guidelines on Ecosystem-based Approaches to Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction. Here, the inclusion of sufficient social and environmental safeguards in climate mitigation-related approaches is pivotal.

Many of the important political implications will concern equity and the relationship between climate and biodiversity finance. COP17 can define steps to ensure that climate-related biodiversity finance is additional, that the same financial flow is not counted toward multiple obligations, and that megadiverse countries as well as communities have access to adequate and predictable finance.

Challenges in implementing Article 8(j) and related provisions

COP16 in Colombia closed with a historic decision: the creation of the Subsidiary Body on Article 8(j) and Other Provisions of the Convention Related to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (SB8J).

Following its first meeting in October 2025, several critical tasks have been referred to COP17, which is expected to adopt the final modus operandi of SB8j, including coordination mechanisms and regional representation. COP17 is also tasked with finalizing the guidelines for operationalizing GBF Targets 2 and 3, ensuring that respect for traditional knowledge and territorial rights is built into their implementation.

COP17 should take steps to ensure that the new Article 8(j) architecture provides more than an enhanced consultation mechanism for Indigenous Peoples and local communities. It should reflect a meaningful shift in the implementation of the Convention toward genuine recognition of their rights, governance, knowledge systems, customary use and collective action.

This work will cut across many of the CBD’s discussions. But many relevant provisions remain bracketed or voluntary, and their effectiveness will depend heavily on finance, national policy and the extent to which Article 8(j) is mainstreamed into implementation.

Unresolved DSI issues

COP16 adopted a multilateral mechanism, including the Cali Fund, which Parties may use as a means of receiving fair and equitable benefits from the use of digital sequence information (DSI) on genetic resources.

However, significant gaps remain. There is no legal certainty that users of DSI will share benefits, nor is there adequate support to ensure that DSI is made available in compliance with applicable national laws. The initial modalities are intended to provide some predictability for monetary benefit-sharing, but early trends are not encouraging. There is also very little information on non-monetary benefits facilitated to date. Meanwhile, critical follow-up work to ensure that DSI is shared with all Parties in a transparent and accountable manner is lagging.

COP17 will face an underlying stalemate: developed countries and industry seek to avoid additional national access and benefit-sharing obligations, while developing countries seek stronger database accountability and transparency to ensure that DSI from their territories is not inequitably extracted through databases in developed countries. Yet COP17 may not address this, as several unresolved issues concerning the operationalization of the Cali Fund remain.

Safeguarding precaution

The precautionary approach is central to the CBD but is being challenged in biosafety discussions. COP17 will consider a Thematic Action Plan to support capacity-building, technology transfer and knowledge sharing in the context of synthetic biology. Parties have a choice: support precaution and focus on capacity-building for assessment and regulatory oversight, or succumb to the push to promote technology transfer and research, despite little evidence of current or potential benefits. The former would help equip developing countries to make sovereign decisions, while not leaving them bearing the burden of any damage or technology failures.

Under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, similar challenges abound. Several topics are proposed for further risk assessment guidance for living modified organisms (LMOs). Any guidance must align with the Protocol’s precautionary approach and must not use industry-aligned methods that weaken and narrow risk assessment. Additionally, the question of whether new genome-edited LMOs fall under the Protocol needs urgent resolution. The continued relevance of the Protocol rests on its ability to maintain precautionary oversight of novel technologies while ensuring that risks don’t fall disproportionately on developing countries or communities.

Success at COP17 rests less on closing the “implementation gap” and more on making progress in addressing the root causes of biodiversity destruction, and placing equity, precaution and protection of the rights of Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women and youth at the center of action, thereby closing the “justice gap”. Only then can biodiversity destruction be effectively halted.  

With input from colleagues at the Third World Network.
items.title: Moving Beyond the Implementation Gap at CBD COP17 Analysis The 2026 UN Biodiversity Conference convenes in Yerevan, Armenia, in mid-October. The key question: will Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), meeting at their Conference of the Parties (COP17), take effective action to stop biodiversity destruction? Mirna Inés Fernández
