The United Nations Office for Partnerships marked the International Day of Democracy with the launch of the second edition of the Handbook on Citizens' Assemblies, a practical resource designed to support governments, civil society organizations and practitioners in strengthening citizen participation through deliberative democratic processes.

The updated handbook, developed by the newDemocracy Foundation with support from the United Nations Democracy Fund (UNDEF) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), provides guidance on the design and implementation of citizens' assemblies and other deliberative democratic mechanisms. Drawing on expanding international experience and lessons learned from practitioners worldwide, the publication aims to help decision-makers create more inclusive, participatory and trusted forms of governance.

The launch took place during a discussion at the Goals Lounge convened by the United Nations Office for Partnerships under the theme, "Raising hands and voices: fostering agency and ownership through deliberative democracy." The event brought together government representatives, civil society organizations, democracy practitioners and multilateral partners to explore how deliberative democratic processes can strengthen citizen agency, public trust and inclusive decision-making.

In his message marking the International Day of Democracy, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized that democracy extends beyond elections and depends on the meaningful participation of people in public affairs.

Opening remarks were delivered by UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed. The discussion also featured representatives from the Permanent Missions of France and the Republic of Korea to the United Nations, alongside speakers from CIVICUS, UNDP and the newDemocracy Foundation.

Participants shared examples of how citizens' assemblies and other deliberative processes are being used around the world to address complex policy challenges, improve public trust and create more responsive governance systems. The discussion highlighted growing international recognition of the importance of meaningful public participation in strengthening democratic resilience and improving policy outcomes.

The release of the updated handbook reflects increasing global interest in deliberative democracy and provides a timely resource for policymakers and practitioners seeking practical approaches to engaging citizens in decision-making processes.

Debates over China’s industrial advancement are often framed around the narrative of “forced technology transfer.” The history of China’s heavy-duty gas turbine sector—a cornerstone of global power generation—tells a more nuanced story. Rather than administrative coercion, it reveals a process shaped by calculated risk management, strategic bargaining, and negotiated asymmetry. As the European Union and China deepen their engagement in clean technologies such as wind power, photovoltaics, energy storage, and hydrogen, this history offers pragmatic insights for building resilient partnerships grounded in mutual interests, beyond reductive ideological framings.

Commercial Drivers and Negotiated Outcomes 

Beginning in 2001, China sought to address a technological gap in heavy-duty gas turbines following decades of underinvestment. To facilitate this, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) implemented a "bundled bidding" (打捆招标) mechanism, consolidating fragmented provincial demand into substantial orders—totaling over 50 units and approximately 20 gigawatts of capacity between 2001 and 2007. These contracts supported three major consortia: Harbin Electric with GE, Dongfang Electric with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and Shanghai Electric with Siemens.

While often viewed through the lens of market access requirements, the internal dynamics of these Joint Ventures (JVs) reflect standard international commercial practices. Foreign partners structured the deals to retain decisive control. A notable example is the Shanghai Electric-Siemens joint venture established in 2005, in which Siemens held a 51 percent majority stake against Shanghai Electric’s 49 percent. This equity structure translated directly into operational authority. Crucially, the scope of technology transfer was explicitly defined and contractually ring-fenced from the outset.

Foreign entities maintained distinct control over several key areas. Software designing, controlling system source codes, and core algorithms remained the exclusive property of the foreign parent company. Chinese engineers were granted production licenses—the right to manufacture to specification—while the underlying design rationale remained protected. Manufacturing processes for critical components, including single-crystal turbine blades and combustion chambers, were generally excluded from transfer agreements, with these items typically sourced from facilities in Germany, the United States, or Japan. Foreign firms also retained oversight of maintenance, repairs, and overhauls (MRO), utilizing proprietary diagnostic systems.

This structure allowed multinationals to capture significant lifecycle value through licensing fees, component sales, and service agreements. Rather than reflecting a unilateral concession, these arrangements enabled multinational firms to protect high-value intellectual property while leveraging China’s manufacturing capacities. The available evidence indicates these were calculated business decisions balancing market access against competitive preservation.

At the same time, Western firms faced strong commercial incentives. During the early 2000s, China represented a primary growth market for power generation. Investments such as GE’s Qinhuangdao Energy Service Center in 2004 underscore the commercial rationale behind local partnerships. The technology shared was largely mature, enabling firms to extend the profitability lifecycle of existing designs. For Chinese stakeholders, these agreements offered a pathway to acquire advanced manufacturing qualifications and accumulate engineering experience, even if core IP remained protected. The resulting arrangements represented a negotiated trade-off: market access in exchange for manufacturing know-how, with both sides accepting asymmetry to secure their respective strategic objectives.

The Strategic Pivot to Indigenous Innovation 

The gas turbine experience also exposes the limitations of relying solely on joint ventures for acquiring core technological mastery. By the late 2000s, it became apparent within China’s industrial planning that while manufacturing capabilities had improved, fundamental competencies in materials science and aerodynamic design remained elusive through commercial partnerships alone.

Recognizing these limitations, China gradually shifted its strategy from acquiring manufacturing capabilities through joint venture toward strengthening indigenous innovation. In 2012, China launched the "Aero Engine and Gas Turbine" Major National Science and Technology Project (the "Two Machines" project). This initiative signaled a shift toward substantial, state-supported indigenous R&D. 

Subsequent developments, such as Dongfang Electric’s announcement in 2024 regarding the full-load operation of its independent F-class 50-megawatt gas turbine, illustrate progress in domestic capability. Additionally, Shanghai Electric’s 2014 acquisition of a 40 percent stake in Italy’s Ansaldo Energia provided access to an alternative Western technology stack. These trajectories suggest that while joint ventures offer a double-edged sword—providing immediate industrial capacity but potentially limiting access to core secrets—long-term technological sovereignty often necessitates autonomous innovation pathways.

Toward a Collaborative Clean Tech Framework 

Today's clean technology sectors differ significantly from the gas turbine industry two decades ago. However, the underlying challenge remains the same: how to balance market access, intellectual property protection, industrial competitiveness, and long-term innovation. The gas turbine experience therefore provides a useful historical lens through which current EU-China cooperation can be reassessed.

As the EU and China expand cooperation into wind, solar, storage, and hydrogen, the gas turbine precedent offers constructive parallels. Moving forward, the focus might shift from ideological debates toward institutional design that acknowledges mutual dependencies.

Clear and well-defined intellectual property arrangements remain essential. Future frameworks could explicitly distinguish between background IP, foreground IP generated through collaboration, and process-related knowledge. Establishing clear parameters for data governance and technology usage upfront can mitigate misunderstandings. Furthermore, recognizing that successful cooperation requires balancing technological openness with the protection of legitimate commercial interests can foster more sustainable partnerships.

Collaboration in third-country markets presents another avenue. By combining European technological depth with Chinese manufacturing scale, EU-China consortia could undertake renewable energy projects in emerging economies. Such "third-market" cooperation aligns with both the EU’s Global Gateway and China’s Belt and Road Initiative, transforming potential bilateral friction into shared commercial and developmental opportunities.

Conclusion: Navigating Trade-offs for a Net-Zero Future 

While economic security concerns are reshaping industrial policies on both sides, the gas turbine experience suggests that commercial cooperation and strategic competition need not be mutually exclusive. Characterizing technology exchange solely through narratives of coercion or victimhood overlooks the agency of all parties involved. Similarly, expecting joint ventures to automatically bridge profound technological gaps underestimates the protective instincts inherent in competitive markets.

As the EU and China pursue a net-zero future, moving beyond adversarial framings is crucial. By prioritizing equitable, risk-sharing models and transparent contractual frameworks, both sides can cultivate a clean tech ecosystem that drives innovation while respecting commercial realities. The objective is not to eliminate competition but to manage it through rules that incentivize investment and protect legitimate interests. The gas turbine legacy demonstrates that technology cooperation is a dynamic process involving continuous negotiation and trade-offs. Applying these lessons to today’s clean technology sectors can help transform potential friction into a productive partnership that supports the global energy transition.

items.title: Beyond “Forced Transfer”: Commercial Lessons for EU-China Clean Tech Cooperation Analysis China’s heavy-duty gas turbine industry offers a more complex story than the familiar narrative of “forced technology transfer” — one shaped by commercial bargaining, market access and negotiated interests. As the EU and China navigate growing competition. Prof. Li Zheng
items.summary:
Debates over China’s industrial advancement are often framed around the narrative of “forced technology transfer.” The history of China’s heavy-duty gas turbine sector—a cornerstone of global power generation—tells a more nuanced story. Rather than administrative coercion, it reveals a process shaped by calculated risk management, strategic bargaining, and negotiated asymmetry. As the European Union and China deepen their engagement in clean technologies such as wind power, photovoltaics, energy storage, and hydrogen, this history offers pragmatic insights for building resilient partnerships grounded in mutual interests, beyond reductive ideological framings.

Commercial Drivers and Negotiated Outcomes 

Beginning in 2001, China sought to address a technological gap in heavy-duty gas turbines following decades of underinvestment. To facilitate this, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) implemented a "bundled bidding" (打捆招标) mechanism, consolidating fragmented provincial demand into substantial orders—totaling over 50 units and approximately 20 gigawatts of capacity between 2001 and 2007. These contracts supported three major consortia: Harbin Electric with GE, Dongfang Electric with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and Shanghai Electric with Siemens.

While often viewed through the lens of market access requirements, the internal dynamics of these Joint Ventures (JVs) reflect standard international commercial practices. Foreign partners structured the deals to retain decisive control. A notable example is the Shanghai Electric-Siemens joint venture established in 2005, in which Siemens held a 51 percent majority stake against Shanghai Electric’s 49 percent. This equity structure translated directly into operational authority. Crucially, the scope of technology transfer was explicitly defined and contractually ring-fenced from the outset.

Foreign entities maintained distinct control over several key areas. Software designing, controlling system source codes, and core algorithms remained the exclusive property of the foreign parent company. Chinese engineers were granted production licenses—the right to manufacture to specification—while the underlying design rationale remained protected. Manufacturing processes for critical components, including single-crystal turbine blades and combustion chambers, were generally excluded from transfer agreements, with these items typically sourced from facilities in Germany, the United States, or Japan. Foreign firms also retained oversight of maintenance, repairs, and overhauls (MRO), utilizing proprietary diagnostic systems.

This structure allowed multinationals to capture significant lifecycle value through licensing fees, component sales, and service agreements. Rather than reflecting a unilateral concession, these arrangements enabled multinational firms to protect high-value intellectual property while leveraging China’s manufacturing capacities. The available evidence indicates these were calculated business decisions balancing market access against competitive preservation.

At the same time, Western firms faced strong commercial incentives. During the early 2000s, China represented a primary growth market for power generation. Investments such as GE’s Qinhuangdao Energy Service Center in 2004 underscore the commercial rationale behind local partnerships. The technology shared was largely mature, enabling firms to extend the profitability lifecycle of existing designs. For Chinese stakeholders, these agreements offered a pathway to acquire advanced manufacturing qualifications and accumulate engineering experience, even if core IP remained protected. The resulting arrangements represented a negotiated trade-off: market access in exchange for manufacturing know-how, with both sides accepting asymmetry to secure their respective strategic objectives.

The Strategic Pivot to Indigenous Innovation 

The gas turbine experience also exposes the limitations of relying solely on joint ventures for acquiring core technological mastery. By the late 2000s, it became apparent within China’s industrial planning that while manufacturing capabilities had improved, fundamental competencies in materials science and aerodynamic design remained elusive through commercial partnerships alone.

Recognizing these limitations, China gradually shifted its strategy from acquiring manufacturing capabilities through joint venture toward strengthening indigenous innovation. In 2012, China launched the "Aero Engine and Gas Turbine" Major National Science and Technology Project (the "Two Machines" project). This initiative signaled a shift toward substantial, state-supported indigenous R&D. 

Subsequent developments, such as Dongfang Electric’s announcement in 2024 regarding the full-load operation of its independent F-class 50-megawatt gas turbine, illustrate progress in domestic capability. Additionally, Shanghai Electric’s 2014 acquisition of a 40 percent stake in Italy’s Ansaldo Energia provided access to an alternative Western technology stack. These trajectories suggest that while joint ventures offer a double-edged sword—providing immediate industrial capacity but potentially limiting access to core secrets—long-term technological sovereignty often necessitates autonomous innovation pathways.

Toward a Collaborative Clean Tech Framework 

Today's clean technology sectors differ significantly from the gas turbine industry two decades ago. However, the underlying challenge remains the same: how to balance market access, intellectual property protection, industrial competitiveness, and long-term innovation. The gas turbine experience therefore provides a useful historical lens through which current EU-China cooperation can be reassessed.

As the EU and China expand cooperation into wind, solar, storage, and hydrogen, the gas turbine precedent offers constructive parallels. Moving forward, the focus might shift from ideological debates toward institutional design that acknowledges mutual dependencies.

Such "third-market" cooperation aligns with both the EU’s Global Gateway and China’s Belt and Road Initiative, transforming potential bilateral friction into shared commercial and developmental opportunities.

The EU-China trade debate is heating up. Just before the summer break, European leaders are considering new measures to address widening economic imbalances with China. Yet as Europe debates how to reduce its trade deficit and dependence on Chinese clean tech, the continent itself is also heating up. And Chinese technology, in the form of air conditioners, is providing some much-needed relief.

Beijing Sees Air Conditioners as a Trade Success Story

June 2026 was the hottest June on record in western Europe. During the heatwave, temperatures across France, Germany, Italy and Spain reached between 5°C and 12°C above seasonal averages. Demand for air conditioners surged, and a large part of the demand is met by Chinese manufacturers: Chinese air conditioners exports to the EU rose by 43 percent year on year in the first half of 2026. Leading Chinese home appliance brand Midea’s reported that sales of its PortaSplit model, a portable split system unit adapted to western European window designs and building regulations, sold more than 200,000 in Europe so far this year, twice the level recorded a year earlier.

Chinese state media have, rightly so, presented the surge in Chinese air conditioner sales as a tangible benefit of EU-China trade: a classic case of comparative advantage and the fundamental “win-win” nature of the EU-China economic relationship. China’s industrial specialisation, supply chain efficiency and technological competitiveness have enabled it to provide products that help Europe adapt to intensifying climate shocks.

European policymakers, however, will have some doubts on the broader conclusion drawn from this argument: that de-risking or trade defense measures to address Chinese economic imbalances and supply chain dependence amount to little more than a game of “cold statistics” that will ultimately hurt ordinary consumers. This framing presents the growth in air conditioner sales as evidence that European consumers’ growing preference for Chinese products and market efficiency should outweigh European concerns about trade imbalances and industrial dependence.

In think-tank exchanges, Chinese interlocutors frequently invoke comparative advantage to explain the benefits of deeper EU-China climate cooperation. Europe, they argue, should take advantage of China’s manufacturing strength in solar panels, electric vehicles, batteries and wind technology to accelerate its energy transition and drive down soaring energy bills for consumers. 

Yet this logic does not fully capture the strategic questions now confronting European policymakers. Two issues are particularly important: whether economic efficiency should still take precedence over strategic resilience, and Europe’s ability to pursue the same supply chain resilience policies that China has long sought for itself.

Europe Is Prioritising Economic Security Over Trade Efficiency

On the first issue, David Ricardo’s economic theory from the 19th century is insufficient as a guide to policy in our changing world. Comparative advantage is premised on maximising economic efficiency. Yet the past decade has shown that the conditions needed to keep this system running smoothly can no longer be taken for granted.

The shocks have taught Europe about the costs of concentrated dependence.

The shortage of personal protective equipment during Covid-19, Europe’s exposure to Russian gas dependency following the Kremlin’s decision to invade Ukraine, the disruption caused by Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, the severe disruption to European supply chains caused by China’s rare earth export restrictions in response to US tariffs, and the Strait of Hormuz energy crisis triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran are only some of the shocks that have taught Europe about the costs of concentrated dependence. 

These crises have shown that contingency and redundancy, rather than economic efficiency alone, are increasingly important to the basic functioning of society. As Europe navigates “changes unseen in a century”, diversification and localisation are not an irrational rejection of free trade. It is the logical choice for business and responsible course for governments seeking to avoid economically expedient but strategically exposed reliance on a small number of concentrated suppliers.

China grasped this strategic lesson earlier than Europe: supply chains must be able to function under extreme conditions. In articulating the dual-circulation strategy during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, President Xi described the crisis as a stress test for China’s industrial supply chains. He argued that China should establish alternative sources and build self-reliant, controllable, secure and reliable domestic production systems in areas connected to national security. 

This logic was subsequently embedded in China’s 14th (and 15th) Five-year Plan, new critical infrastructure legislation and in major energy sector policies. For example, a National Energy Administration document published in 2025 calls for greater control over the technologies underpinning the energy value chain and set an explicit target for the supply chains of key energy equipment to be “self-reliant and controllable” by 2030.

The Future of EU–China Trade Depends on Supply Chain Resilience

And this brings us to the second issue: reciprocity. As one CGTN commentary acknowledged, “every economy has a legitimate interest in safeguarding critical industries and strengthening supply-chain resilience”. China has long translated that interest into policy. The EU is now doing the same by raising the questions that Chinese policymakers raised years ago: which industrial and technological capabilities must continue to exist within Europe? Which may become essential in a crisis? And what would happen if access to them were suddenly disrupted?

The diversification provisions of the Net Zero Industry Act reflect this logic. Just as no major economy would willingly rely on a single or highly concentrated group of suppliers for fossil fuels, Europe has decided that no single external supplier country should account for more than half of EU supply of strategic net zero technologies. Renewable technologies are, of course, different from fossil fuels. Wind and sunlight cannot be switched off, but access to the resource is not the same as having the equipment, software, engineering and maintenance capacity needed to harness it. A country with oil reserves but no drilling capability is not energy secure. The same applies to renewable energy.

The Industrial Accelerator Act is intended to create the conditions in which Europe can retain and rebuild some of these industrial capabilities, through incentives to localisation production, national ownership conditions, and technology transfer requirements. Foreign companies operating in China have long faced similar demands, which has partly contributed to China’s industrial development in sectors such as wind and electric vehicles, an earlier model of “win-win” cooperation that Beijing might now recognise in Europe’s own approach.

Beijing has spent years deciding which capabilities China cannot afford to lose. Europe is now asking the same question.

Viewed from this perspective, the raft of incoming trade defence and industrial policy measures by the EU should not be understood as Europe abandoning free trade or cooperation, it is, rather, a response to a more volatile world that has shaped Beijing’s own pursuit of self-reliance. 

Chinese air conditioners may demonstrate the “win-win” model of trade working as intended. Comparative advantage can continue to shape where trade is beneficial, but those benefits cannot override the wider questions of strategic autonomy, energy security and supply chain resilience. Beijing has spent years deciding which capabilities China cannot afford to lose. Europe is now asking the same question. 

The question for the future of EU-China trade and economic relations is therefore whether both sides are prepared to recognise the same strategic logic on industrial development and economic security, identify the areas in which economic security will trump efficiency, and, on that basis, preserve the areas in which trade remains mutually beneficial.

LONDON, UNITED KINGDOM – 11 SEPTEMBER 2026 

A new commission by Aziza Kadyri, Sender Unknown, is now on view in The Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A), following its unveiling today, as part of London Design Festival 2026 as well as the Museum’s Jameel programme, celebrating 20 years of The Jameel Gallery with Community Jameel. The display will remain on view until 10 January 2027.

A London-based artist of Uzbek origin, Kadyri brings suzani, a traditional Central Asian type of embroidery, into dialogue with artificial intelligence (AI) and digital textile printing. Using a bespoke AI model and drawing on motifs from traditional examples together with contemporary experience, Kadyri has developed a new language of suzani symbols, which have been hand-embroidered onto fabric by skilled women artisans in Nurota, Uzbekistan.

Suzani is a living craft tradition practised across Central Asia, particularly in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, with distinctive regional styles and techniques. Traditionally made by women, often as part of a bride’s dowry, suzani embroidery is now experiencing renewed interest, with artisans, artists and designers bringing its techniques and visual language into contemporary practice.

By combining AI with hand embroidery, Sender Unknown explores how cultural knowledge is translated across technologies and generations. The work does not reproduce historic suzani designs, but rather uses new technology to generate contemporary motifs that are interpreted and brought to life through the skill of women artisans. The installation explores the dialogue between long standing approaches to the translation and borrowing of design language with the extractive and homogenising processes which underpin generative AI models. Through this dialogue, and through the collaboration between the artist, artisans, and AI models, Sender Unknown shows how communities can regain agency and harness this technology in the present.

Sender Unknown will be accompanied by suzani embroidery workshops led by Yulduz Mukhiddinova, the Uzbek embroiderer who collaborated with Kadyri on the commission. Two sessions will take place at The Jameel Gallery on Wednesday 16 September, with two additional sessions taking place on Friday 18 September as part of V&A x London Design Festival: Awakenings Friday Late. The workshops will introduce visitors to the history and motifs of suzani followed by a practical embroidery session using traditional motifs and the contemporary motifs developed by Kadyri.

The display is a reflection of the geographical breadth of Islamic art collections represented in The Jameel Gallery, which span from Spain and North Africa through the Middle East, Iran and Turkey to Central Asia, including Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. The V&A holds an important collection of historic suzani, including a nineteenth-century example from Uzbekistan.

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: “For 20 years, The Jameel Gallery has offered the public a  greater understanding of the artistic traditions of the Islamic world. Sender Unknown continues this work by bringing historic collections, living craft traditions and contemporary creative practice into conversation. Community Jameel is pleased to support work that creates opportunities for traditional craftsmanship to be practised, shared, and reinterpreted for new generations.”

Sender Unknown is the latest activity in a special programme marking 20 years of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A with Community Jameel. The anniversary programme has included The Art of Egyptian Khayamiyya, with master Egyptian tentmaker Hany Abd El-Kader; Golden Threads: Dress from Saudi Arabia, a temporary display of rare mid-twentieth-century traditional Saudi garments; The Islamic Art Museumscape, a conference exploring current trends and issues affecting the presentation of Islamic art in museums; and the Gallery’s 20th anniversary celebration hosted by Community Jameel at the V&A on 23 July, attended by HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal and members of the Jameel family, featuring traditional craft demonstrations and a performance by the London Arab Orchestra, which was formally designated the inaugural event in the official lead-up to the 2029 UK-Saudi Year of Culture.

This commission display is a reflection of Community Jameel’s wider commitment to sustaining traditional craftsmanship through education, training, and opportunities for craftspeople to pass on their skills. Community Jameel has partnered with The King’s Foundation School of Traditional Arts to establish the Jameel Houses of Traditional Arts, a network of schools in Cairo, Jeddah and Scotland that offer emerging artists and craftspeople training in traditional arts alongside pathways to professional practice.

LONDON, UNITED KINGDOM – 11 SEPTEMBER 2026 

A new commission by Aziza Kadyri, Sender Unknown, is now on view in The Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A), following its unveiling today, as part of London Design Festival 2026 as well as the Museum’s Jameel programme, celebrating 20 years of The Jameel Gallery with Community Jameel. The display will remain on view until 10 January 2027.

A London-based artist of Uzbek origin, Kadyri brings suzani, a traditional Central Asian type of embroidery, into dialogue with artificial intelligence (AI) and digital textile printing. Using a bespoke AI model and drawing on motifs from traditional examples together with contemporary experience, Kadyri has developed a new language of suzani symbols, which have been hand-embroidered onto fabric by skilled women artisans in Nurota, Uzbekistan.

Suzani is a living craft tradition practised across Central Asia, particularly in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, with distinctive regional styles and techniques. Traditionally made by women, often as part of a bride’s dowry, suzani embroidery is now experiencing renewed interest, with artisans, artists and designers bringing its techniques and visual language into contemporary practice.

By combining AI with hand embroidery, Sender Unknown explores how cultural knowledge is translated across technologies and generations. The work does not reproduce historic suzani designs, but rather uses new technology to generate contemporary motifs that are interpreted and brought to life through the skill of women artisans. The installation explores the dialogue between long standing approaches to the translation and borrowing of design language with the extractive and homogenising processes which underpin generative AI models. Through this dialogue, and through the collaboration between the artist, artisans, and AI models, Sender Unknown shows how communities can regain agency and harness this technology in the present.

Sender Unknown will be accompanied by suzani embroidery workshops led by Yulduz Mukhiddinova, the Uzbek embroiderer who collaborated with Kadyri on the commission. Two sessions will take place at The Jameel Gallery on Wednesday 16 September, with two additional sessions taking place on Friday 18 September as part of V&A x London Design Festival: Awakenings Friday Late. The workshops will introduce visitors to the history and motifs of suzani followed by a practical embroidery session using traditional motifs and the contemporary motifs developed by Kadyri.

The display is a reflection of the geographical breadth of Islamic art collections represented in The Jameel Gallery, which span from Spain and North Africa through the Middle East, Iran and Turkey to Central Asia, including Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. The V&A holds an important collection of historic suzani, including a nineteenth-century example from Uzbekistan.

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: “For 20 years, The Jameel Gallery has offered the public a  greater understanding of the artistic traditions of the Islamic world. Sender Unknown continues this work by bringing historic collections, living craft traditions and contemporary creative practice into conversation. Community Jameel is pleased to support work that creates opportunities for traditional craftsmanship to be practised, shared, and reinterpreted for new generations.”

Sender Unknown is the latest activity in a special programme marking 20 years of The Jameel Gallery at the V&A with Community Jameel. The anniversary programme has included The Art of Egyptian Khayamiyya, with master Egyptian tentmaker Hany Abd El-Kader; Golden Threads: Dress from Saudi Arabia, a temporary display of rare mid-twentieth-century traditional Saudi garments; The Islamic Art Museumscape, a conference exploring current trends and issues affecting the presentation of Islamic art in museums; and the Gallery’s 20th anniversary celebration hosted by Community Jameel at the V&A on 23 July, attended by HRH Prince Turki Al-Faisal and members of the Jameel family, featuring traditional craft demonstrations and a performance by the London Arab Orchestra, which was formally designated the inaugural event in the official lead-up to the 2029 UK-Saudi Year of Culture.

This commission display is a reflection of Community Jameel’s wider commitment to sustaining traditional craftsmanship through education, training, and opportunities for craftspeople to pass on their skills. Community Jameel has partnered with The King’s Foundation School of Traditional Arts to establish the Jameel Houses of Traditional Arts, a network of schools in Cairo, Jeddah and Scotland that offer emerging artists and craftspeople training in traditional arts alongside pathways to professional practice.

Improved central-local relations are crucial for any future peace process in Yemen.

Under the slogan “take your mattress to the street”, citizens of Aden were sleeping in the middle of the road this summer. Others blocked strategic routes by burning tyres to protest the lack of electricity. In the past months, residents were lucky when they got two hours of electricity a day in the unbearable summer heat.

Electricity is not their only concern: water networks, sewage systems, street cleaning, and garbage collection are also not consistently available in Aden and beyond. As basic services remain often unreliable, Yemeni citizens’ frustration is growing.

Since taking office in February, the new government has taken several measures to address the situation. It has sought to streamline governance and security by placing them under one leadership in areas under its control, while promising to improve living conditions. It has also driven important economic reforms aimed at enhancing the economic and financial situation.

Overlapping competencies of local and central authorities

While these efforts may show results in the medium term, in the short term, local authorities continue to step in where the central government has been unable to provide. Often with support of international donors, and in some cases the Yemeni private sector, they have pursued ad hoc fixes for the most pressing local needs: rehabilitating water networks, renovating schools, and building or upgrading health centres. At the same time, local authorities have come up with economic development plans for their governorate, which outline their needs and opportunities, demonstrating their ambition and capacity to govern responsibly.

Unfortunately, these parallel efforts at central and local levels are sometimes in tension. Governorates with their own natural resources, such as Hadhramawt or Marib, have retained some or all their revenues rather than transferring them to the central level, allowing them to cover their substantial needs, while prompting criticism from the cash-strapped central government. Other governorates complain that budget allocations they are supposed to be receiving from the central government have not been received in years. In recent weeks, disputes have also emerged in Aden and Lahj over political appointments and which level of government has the authority to make them.

Rather than acting as partners in the country’s development, the two levels have increasingly become competitors for power and resources. Competencies are disputed and while the state pushes for greater oversight and control of funds, governorates complain that they are not receiving the support they need.

Need for constructive dialogue and cooperation

More dialogue between central and local levels is essential. Meetings between governors and the Ministry of Local Administration, for example, take place only when funding is available and, at best, once a year.

There is also a need to agree on the rules of the game. Should the government strive to restore the level of centralisation that existed prior to the outbreak of the war, more than a decade ago? Would governorates agree? Should Local Authority Law No. 4 of 2000 be fully implemented, with laws and practices that contravene it being eliminated? Or should more of the de facto arrangements that have emerged in the last few years be formalised and regularised? How can a state that remains legally highly centralised, but contends with high levels of de facto decentralisation, function better?

The recent ‘National Conference for Partnership and Integration’, held in Aden in mid-June 2026, was a first step towards addressing these questions and launching a more constructive dialogue. It was organised by the Ministry of Local Administration with political backing from the President of the Presidential Leadership Council and the Prime Minister, with support from the Berghof Foundation and our local partner, the Political Development Forum.

The conference built on a survey examining key challenges and overlaps between the central and local levels in judicial and administrative affairs, development, resources and finance, as well as two preparatory workshops involving relevant line ministries and technical experts from the governorates. It aimed at identifying areas of existing agreement and outstanding differences. Participants recommended establishing a Higher Joint Coordination Council to continue the dialogue and develop an implementation framework that is realistic, sustainable, and workable for both sides.

The conference also highlighted that substantial disagreements around the relationship between the central and local authorities remain, with some ministries raising fundamental objections to the proposed reform agenda.

Coherent and effective governance is essential for peace

Agreement on revenues and other core issues will likely require more sustained dialogue between central and local authorities in the months and years ahead. All sides agree that such a process is necessary. However, it will require greater trust as well as recognition that decentralisation can ultimately benefit both the central government and local authorities. More coherent and effective governance, and a state capable of delivering basic services will also be needed to make any potential peace agreement stick.

After all, political discussions should remain focused on what matters most: easing citizens’ hardship and improving basic services. If the image of people taking their mattresses to the streets during Aden’s summer heat remains in the minds of decision-makers, it may help keep the process constructive and focused on tangible results.

items.content_html:
Funding is political.

Who decides where resources go matters, and, too often, funding decisions are made far from the communities most impacted by injustice. Participatory grantmaking challenges this approach by shifting decision-making closer to the people leading change.

Our new report, Participatory Grantmaking with Feminist Movements: Reflections on Power and Practice, reflects on five years of Global Fund for Women's experience supporting feminist movements with participatory grantmaking, and what we learned along the way.

The report explores how participatory grantmaking can strengthen movements, expand access to funding for historically under-resourced groups, and deepen trust. It also surfaces the tensions, tradeoffs, and complexities that come with shifting power via participatory grantmaking.

As movements continue organizing for justice under increasingly difficult conditions, philanthropy must also evolve, trusting movements not only to lead change, but to shape how resources flow and how success is defined.

Whether you are a funder, movement leader, researcher, or advocate, this report offers practical insights into building more equitable partnerships with movements driving change.

AMMAN, JORDAN – 10 SEPTEMBER 2026 

Representatives from the Greater Amman Municipality, the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, and Community Jameel inaugurated today a new tactical urbanism project along Al-Taj Street in Amman’s Al-Yarmouk District. The pilot project demonstrates how rapid, low-cost urban transformations can protect residents from extreme heat while creating safer, more welcoming spaces for children, students, and local families.

The Al-Taj Street pilot forms part of the work by the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel, which works directly with the cities of Amman and Chennai to align their spatial plans and land-use policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data to deliver more sustainable, people-centred urban environments. The Labs have helped shape 15 urban planning policies, regulations and municipal strategies. In total, these policy and planning initiatives directly reach 4.5 million people, including 2.52 million climate-vulnerable residents across Amman.

Tactical urbanism uses short-term, low-cost, and scalable interventions to test long-term spatial change. Data collected through monitoring and evaluation of the site following the pilot’s inauguration will be analysed to inform future neighbourhood upgrading projects across Amman.

Delivered through the Jameel C40 Labs, the pilot reimagines two vulnerable sites along the congested Al-Taj Street corridor. By targeting a major school crossing for four schools and a central traffic island, the project turns key stretches of exposed asphalt into shaded, community-centred-public space.

Co-designed directly with local residents, the transformation delivers immediate climate solutions alongside vital community benefits: 

  • A cooler, safer school zone: Bright, heat-reflective street art now transforms dark asphalt at school gates, lowering surface temperatures while slowing traffic to protect students on their journey to and from school.

  • Shaded waiting and social spaces: New shade canopies, climbing green trellises, and native drought-tolerant planters offer cool, comfortable resting spots for residents.

  • Safe spaces for play: Children in the neighbourhood now have a dedicated, 250m2 play area placed safely away from heavy traffic, featuring custom climbing structures built from recycled materials.

  • Community pride and stewardship: Over 100m2 of vibrant wall murals were painted by local youth and volunteer groups, fostering the long-term community stewardship essential for sustained urban transformation.

Ahmad Al-Malkawi, Chairman of the Greater Amman Municipality Committee, said: "The Al-Taj Street project represents a pivotal opportunity to translate urban planning and design principles from a theoretical framework into tangible solutions that respond to the daily needs of residents. This tactical urbanism intervention provides a scalable and replicable model for neighbourhoods across Amman, particularly those most vulnerable to climate impacts. 

Through this participatory approach, we look forward to developing a more resilient, sustainable, and safe urban environment, while fostering accessible, inclusive, and welcoming public spaces in close collaboration with our international partners and the local community.”

George Richards, Director of Community Jameel, said: "Drawing on traditional urbanism practices in the Arab world as well as research and evidence-based design, the Al-Taj Street pilot shows how climate planning can move from strategy into implementation, creating accessible, climate-resilient public spaces for residents. Working closely with Greater Amman Municipality, the Jameel C40 Labs have helped align Amman’s urban planning policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data to deliver more sustainable, people-centred neighbourhoods in the city."

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: "Great urban planning isn't just drawn on paper; it's tested on the streets alongside the people who live there. By combining a deeply people-centred approach with tactical urbanism, the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and Greater Amman Municipality are turning ambitious climate goals into tangible change along Al-Taj street in Al Yarmouk neighbourhood. This project demonstrates how quick, cost-effective interventions can transform asphalt and unshaded public space into vibrant, heat-resilient communities - offering a clear blueprint not just for other neighborhoods across Amman, but for cities across the region."

The Al-Taj Street tactical urbanism project serves as a localised demonstration of the Jameel C40 Labs' broader policy and planning initiatives in Amman. Crucial to this wider effort is supporting the adoption of the Amman Zoning & Planning Bylaw in 2025, which represents a landmark shift for the city by formalising environmental considerations and community participation in urban planning for the very first time.

This legislative framework provides the foundation for neighbourhood-scale action. Building on this, the Jameel C40 Labs developed a climate-responsive neighbourhood plan for Kherbet Al-Souq - also known as Amman’s “Southern Gate” - a five-square-kilometre area expected to grow from around 25,000 residents today to 42,000 by 2050. In May 2026, the plan was formally handed over to the Greater Amman Municipality by the  Jameel C40 Labs, marking an important step in translating the Labs’ climate planning work into a practical framework for managing the neighbourhood’s growth and resilience. The plan focuses on measures including shaded and greener streets, safer walking routes, improved water management, accessible public spaces, climate-smart infrastructure and support for local livelihoods. 

The Al-Taj Street tactical urbanism project is a practical, localised demonstration of this broader neighbourhood approach, showing how climate-responsive planning principles can be translated into immediate, visible improvements while generating lessons that can inform implementation and future neighbourhood planning across Amman.

AMMAN, JORDAN – 9 SEPTEMBER 2026 

The Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, a partnership between C40 Cities and Community Jameel, together with Minecraft Education, the Greater Amman Municipality, and the Queen Rania Centre for Education and Information Technology, awarded  the winning prize of the Schools Reinventing Cities competition to Team Um Tufail from Um Tufail Mixed Secondary School at an official ceremony held today at the Al Hussein Cultural Centre in Amman. 

The competition brought together 97 students across 16 schools over a ten-week design challenge using the digital world of Minecraft Education, a game-based platform developed by the makers of Minecraft, the best-selling video game of all time, in which players use blocks to build and explore infinite worlds.

Through the competition, the students reimagined public spaces in the Al-Yadudah neighbourhood of Amman, with a focus on improving access to healthy food, tackling extreme heat, and creating vibrant, accessible places for play and community life. 

The competition forms part of the wider efforts of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, which work directly with city authorities in Amman and Chennai to align spatial plans and land-use policies with climate targets, emissions pathways and climate risk data. Across both cities, the Labs have helped shape 15 urban planning policies, regulations, and municipal strategies, directly reaching 4.5 million people, including 2.52 million people in Amman.

Schools Reinventing Cities brings this climate planning work into the classroom, giving young people a role in reimagining the public spaces, systems, and climate-resilient neighbourhoods they envision for their city.

The awards ceremony brought together young innovators, city officials, urban planners, and educators to view the winning digital proposals. The teams were assessed based on the quality of their presentations, models, creativity, and the feasibility of implementing their proposals.

Team Um Tufail’s proposal addressed traffic congestion and air pollution, high energy use and waste, lack of green space, and overreliance on private cars in a rapidly growing city. The  proposal included a walkable neighbourhood with public transport, bicycle paths, and electric vehicle charging; solar energy and recycling; parks and natural areas; and connected community services such as a school, library, mosque, and shops. 

The jury found that Team Um Tufail envisioned “a community built around people, nature, and technology, where every area has a purpose and all areas work together as one connected system”. 

Team Eco Builders from Nusaybah Al-Maziniyah Mixed Secondary School came in second place, while the third place award went to Naifa AmmanCraft, from Naifeh First Secondary School for Girls, which presented a project titled Voxel.

The winning team stood out by integrating public transport into its neighbourhood design as a way to reduce emissions and dependence on private cars. The Team Um Tufail project will contribute to implementation of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs’ plan for the wider Kherbet Al-Souq area, which was submitted to the Greater Amman Municipality in May 2026. 

The plan identifies public transport as critical to making its neighbourhoods, including Al-Yadudah, climate responsive, addressing urban sprawl, rising emissions, traffic congestion, and air pollution, while improving equitable access to jobs and services for lower-income households, women, and refugee populations.

Eng. Ziad Abu Arabi, Deputy City Manager for Planning and Economic Development at Greater Amman Municipality, said: “The initiative serves as a vital model for engaging youth in solving real urban and climate challenges, turning their creativity into visions for a greener, more resilient city.” He highlighted that collaboration with C40 Cities, Community Jameel, and local partners aligns Amman's efforts with global best practices, adding that “the initiative's true value lies in the practical skills and experience gained by the students.”

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: "Climate-resilient cities need to be shaped by the people who will live in them. Through the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, Community Jameel is pleased to support work that brings young people into the planning process, giving students in Amman a voice in reimagining safer, greener, and more inclusive neighbourhoods for the future.”

Eng. Muneeb Tashman, Director of the Queen Rania Center for Educational Technology and Information, Ministry of Education, highlighted: “the educational impact of applying Minecraft Education to real-world issues like transit, energy, water, and waste.” He noted that “the partnership reflects the integration of education with sustainable development, cultivating critical thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork among students” while commending the dedication of participating teachers and mentors.

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: "Young people are not just the future of our cities—they are ready to shape them right now. The ingenuity displayed by Amman’s youth in this year’s Schools Reinventing Cities challenge is nothing short of inspiring. By partnering with Community Jameel and Minecraft Education, C40 is proud to provide a platform that unleashes students' creativity, giving them a real voice in how their communities respond to the climate crisis. The ideas celebrated yesterday at the Al Hussein Cultural Centre prove that when students get a say in city building, they design cities that are not only climate-safe, but full of play, community, and possibility."

By proposing practical ways to improve public space, access to healthy food, and climate resilience, the Um Tufail students’ ideas will provide an additional youth perspective to the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and Greater Amman Municipality’s ongoing planning and design process for Kherbet Al-Souq. Additional selected proposals will be shared with the Greater Amman Municipality to help inform future interventions as the neighbourhood develops.

Schools Reinventing Cities brings this climate planning work into the classroom, giving young people a role in reimagining the public spaces, systems, and climate-resilient neighbourhoods they envision for their city.

The awards ceremony brought together young innovators, city officials, urban planners, and educators to view the winning digital proposals. The teams were assessed based on the quality of their presentations, models, creativity, and the feasibility of implementing their proposals.

Team Um Tufail’s proposal addressed traffic congestion and air pollution, high energy use and waste, lack of green space, and overreliance on private cars in a rapidly growing city. The  proposal included a walkable neighbourhood with public transport, bicycle paths, and electric vehicle charging; solar energy and recycling; parks and natural areas; and connected community services such as a school, library, mosque, and shops. 

The jury found that Team Um Tufail envisioned “a community built around people, nature, and technology, where every area has a purpose and all areas work together as one connected system”. 

Team Eco Builders from Nusaybah Al-Maziniyah Mixed Secondary School came in second place, while the third place award went to Naifa AmmanCraft, from Naifeh First Secondary School for Girls, which presented a project titled Voxel.

The winning team stood out by integrating public transport into its neighbourhood design as a way to reduce emissions and dependence on private cars. The Team Um Tufail project will contribute to implementation of the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs’ plan for the wider Kherbet Al-Souq area, which was submitted to the Greater Amman Municipality in May 2026. 

The plan identifies public transport as critical to making its neighbourhoods, including Al-Yadudah, climate responsive, addressing urban sprawl, rising emissions, traffic congestion, and air pollution, while improving equitable access to jobs and services for lower-income households, women, and refugee populations.

Eng. Ziad Abu Arabi, Deputy City Manager for Planning and Economic Development at Greater Amman Municipality, said: “The initiative serves as a vital model for engaging youth in solving real urban and climate challenges, turning their creativity into visions for a greener, more resilient city.” He highlighted that collaboration with C40 Cities, Community Jameel, and local partners aligns Amman's efforts with global best practices, adding that “the initiative's true value lies in the practical skills and experience gained by the students.”

Nader Diab, Head of Programmes at Community Jameel, said: "Climate-resilient cities need to be shaped by the people who will live in them. Through the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs, Community Jameel is pleased to support work that brings young people into the planning process, giving students in Amman a voice in reimagining safer, greener, and more inclusive neighbourhoods for the future.”

Eng. Muneeb Tashman, Director of the Queen Rania Center for Educational Technology and Information, Ministry of Education, highlighted: “the educational impact of applying Minecraft Education to real-world issues like transit, energy, water, and waste.” He noted that “the partnership reflects the integration of education with sustainable development, cultivating critical thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork among students” while commending the dedication of participating teachers and mentors.

Mark Watts, Executive Director of C40 Cities, said: "Young people are not just the future of our cities—they are ready to shape them right now. The ingenuity displayed by Amman’s youth in this year’s Schools Reinventing Cities challenge is nothing short of inspiring. By partnering with Community Jameel and Minecraft Education, C40 is proud to provide a platform that unleashes students' creativity, giving them a real voice in how their communities respond to the climate crisis. The ideas celebrated yesterday at the Al Hussein Cultural Centre prove that when students get a say in city building, they design cities that are not only climate-safe, but full of play, community, and possibility."

By proposing practical ways to improve public space, access to healthy food, and climate resilience, the Um Tufail students’ ideas will provide an additional youth perspective to the Jameel C40 Urban Planning Climate Labs and Greater Amman Municipality’s ongoing planning and design process for Kherbet Al-Souq. Additional selected proposals will be shared with the Greater Amman Municipality to help inform future interventions as the neighbourhood develops.

Ahead of the Berlin Climate and Security Conference, we explore what Germany should do to support the climate, peace, and security agenda.

Climate stress and conflict increasingly overlap. Climate stress does not automatically cause conflict. But where it interacts with weak governance, inequality, and existing instability, it can increase pressure on resources and deepen grievances.

Germany is actively advocating for more support for the climate-security nexus. Yet multiple questions remain around how it can best leverage its position to further advance this cause.

This was the subject of a roundtable on “Climate, peace, and security: Advancing Germany’s policy response”, co-organised with the International Rescue Committee Germany, at our office in Berlin in July. Leading stakeholders from politics, business, academia, and civil society discussed how Germany can more effectively embed climate-related security risks into its national security architecture as well as facilitate access to climate finance for conflict-affected countries.

Berghof’s Executive Director Chris Coulter said Germany “needed to align what already exists far more effectively.” She stressed that climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.

Climate change is not simply a technical issue: it shapes dialogue and mediation and can also provide an entry point for negotiations.Chris Coulter, Executive Director

Connecting climate, peace, and security

For years, climate change and security have been treated as separate issues. Security discussions still follow a conventional military approach. The effects of climate change are not only felt in fragile and conflict-affected countries though but also on supply chains, energy prices, and food security, which have political consequences for Germany and Europe. This framing does not dilute Germany's responsibility or solidarity with the countries hit hardest. However, it makes preventive action politically legible to a wider audience.

The time has come for political leaders to treat climate risk as a core national security priority. A positive sign in this direction was registered at this year’s London Climate Week where climate and nature were framed as systemic risks.

Where the gaps remain

If climate is genuinely treated as a security threat, funding should follow. However, global aid budgets are shrinking. Even if programmes stop running, affected communities still must keep living with the consequences and adapt accordingly. This is compounded by the fact that countries most affected by climate change receive the least funding.

The broader collective-action problem around climate finance also raises a hard question of fairness: who gets left behind? And how do they get brought back into the conversation?

Germany’s policy response

Germany is already playing a leading role in connecting climate, peace, and security. Together with the island state of Nauru, Germany established the UN Group of Friends on Climate and Security with now over 70 Member States. It placed climate security within its Foreign and National Security Strategy and has an advisory commission drawing on civil society expertise, among others. Ahead of this year’s Berlin Climate and Security Conference, the priority should now be to connect existing policies, institutions, and expertise and turn them into practical action.

  • First, Germany should strengthen coordination across foreign policy, development, humanitarian action, climate, and security. Ministries and agencies need shared analysis and clearer objectives, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected countries.

  • Second, Germany should make climate action more conflict sensitive, while ensuring that peacebuilding and humanitarian programmes account for climate pressures. It should also connect high-level diplomacy and mediation more effectively with local authorities and communities.

  • Third, Germany should keep conflict prevention and climate adaptation at the centre of its response. As aid budgets shrink, funding decisions should protect anticipatory action and support communities already facing the combined effects of climate shocks, conflict, and weak governance.

Germany cannot advance this agenda alone. It should continue to work with the United Kingdom, France, and other European partners on shared analysis and coordinated diplomacy. The United Kingdom's new taskforce on nature, climate, and security offers one possible route for exchange. Closer European cooperation would also give Germany’s agenda greater weight in international forums at a time of geopolitical fragmentation and tighter budgets.

Finally, climate security must move beyond its usual policy circles. The case for it needs to be presented in the rooms where decisions on defence, trade, energy and critical minerals are made. Germany has helped build the climate, peace, and security agenda. Its next challenge is to turn that leadership into a joined-up policy that prevents conflict, supports communities, and treats climate resilience as part of security preparedness.

items.content_html:
Séléty and Keur Ayib are two border villages close to Gambia have undergone rapid growth, making them among the most rapidly urbanising areas in Senegal. Both of these villages are located in the Senegambian cross-border area and are known for their cross-border dynamism. Though seemingly peripheral to Senegal’s main urban hubs, these border villages remain closely connected to Gambian towns - making them striking examples of the spatial and socio-economic shifts unfolding in the region.

Indeed, Senegalese rural areas on the border with Gambia are undergoing profound socio-spatial transformation, revealing merging urban dynamic. These shifts are driven by uneven development between town and countryside, eco-geographic disparities and economic potential, which are reshaping internal mobility of Senegalese people.

The Senegal-Gambia Border: A Pump for the Urbanisation of Rural Areas

The dynamics of urbanisation are underpinned by social and spatio-temporal factors: urbanisation can be seen as a phenomenon that transforms society's lifestyles. Over the last few decades, profound changes have occurred in certain Senegalese rural areas along the border with The Gambia, most evidently in the villages like Karang, Séléty and Keur Ayib along the border. This socio-spatial process of urbanisation can be measured in terms of population growth, socio-economic activities and spatial change.

Demographic growth in these villages has reached rates that defied all statistical projections. For example, between 1988 and 2010, the population of Keur Ayib rose from 782 to 4,0001. Beyond natural population growth, rising numbers are largely driven by positive net migration—clear evidence that rural Senegal is undergoing a process of urbanisation.   One effect of the demographic growth was observed by a former mayor of Médina-Sabakh, a commune of which Keur Ayib is one of the largest villages, who said: "Keur Ayib is suffocating and the demand for housing and services is growing by the day. Rapid urbanisation is a real phenomenon and suffers from a lack of planning"2.  

The physical landscape reveals a marked change in the built environment. Over the last few decades, housing has been modernised to keep pace with the arrival of newcomers and new sectors of profitable activity. Senegalese villages are increasingly being built on terraces and on high ground. The findings speak for themselves: 83% of those we surveyed for a study now live in modern housing, while 24% are in transitional dwellings - leaving just 17% in traditional structures.

The rise of modern housing, often built by emerging social classes and rented to civil servants, marks a visible shift in the local landscape. Open, communal living spaces are increasingly giving way to enclosed, individual compounds - a clear sign of an urbanising society where privacy, status, and property boundaries are becoming more prominent.

In addition to this, there is an exponential spread of occupied space. Villages and towns that were once far apart now form a continuum. This rapid and spontaneous occupation of space is creating disorder and insecurity, leading to planning problems.

Border dynamics are driving rural urbanisation in Senegal.

The urbanisation of rural areas in Senegal is essentially due to a crisis in the rural economy and the opportunities offered by secondary towns. Since their creation, the main activity ensuring development in these villages was agriculture. The rural economy, based on working the land and processing its products, occupied the majority of the inhabitants and enabled the farmers to guarantee food self-sufficiency. However, the rural economy suffered a real crisis with the drought of the 1970s and the subsequent deterioration in trade. The search for alternatives led rural dwellers to convert to the trade, craft, tourism and services sectors.

Among the factors that explain the urban dynamic are geographical position, the development of the road network and the low cost of land. Villages located on the border and near secondary towns have benefited from opportunities such as the existence of the road network and the accessibility to land, which have accelerated their urbanisation. The secondary towns have also experienced a demographic boom, accompanied by promiscuity, insecurity, a growing informal sector and a high demand for basic social services. The major consequences of this situation are the saturation of dedicated structures and infrastructure, the disappearance of traditional activities and land speculation, which is a source of conflict between locals and migrants.

Transit areas are the main places of attraction as the large numbers of people passing through these areas make trade and related activities very profitable. The new players need to transform this formerly agricultural space for their housing and the expansion of their activities.

Furthermore, increased consumption and the opportunity to travel to the rest of the country have encouraged the demographic explosion and socio-spatial changes in Senegalese villages located along the Senegal/Gambia border. Proximity to Gambian urban centres - along with differences in currency and cost of living - has fuelled strong ties between town and countryside. These cross-border dynamics are accelerating urbanisation in Senegal’s rural areas, where some villages now function as informal extensions of Gambian cities, serving as commuter hubs or dormitory towns for urban workers.

Political instability and economic hardship have also reshaped Senegal’s rural borderlands. Indeed, the coups d'état in The Gambia and the long-running conflict in the Casamance region are key drivers for migration. Many refugees took advantage of this to acquire land and settle permanently. Another less visible force behind this transformation is “Communitisation”. Communitisation refers to belonging to the same family or ethnic group on which the territory is built, which has led to the formation of socially homogenous neighbourhoods and reinforced local territorial identities3.

The Transformation of City Lifestyles 

The demographic boom, the diversity of business sectors and the presence of civil servants have all contributed to raising living standards. As a result, the landscape has been transformed by changes in housing, the densification and consumption of agricultural land, and the emergence of new lifestyles (food and clothing). The construction of major infrastructure and new housing and service facilities is helping to modernise the built environment in rural areas. With this in mind, the State of Senegal's "one family, one roof" social housing programme, which is being carried out in peri-urban areas, is contributing to the urbanisation of these rural areas. For instance, the planned development of 1,500 plots across 50 hectares in Keur Ayib, along with a five-hectare Customs House project set to include 300 homes, underscores the rapid urbanisation taking place in border areas.

Long waits at border crossings are doing more than slowing travellers - they’re fuelling a boom in informal economic activity that’s reshaping local landscapes. From trade and food stalls to mattress rentals, money transfers, horse-drawn carts and Jakarta motorbikes, these services are thriving and, by many accounts, highly profitable. In recent years, tourism infrastructure has also taken root, turning these transit zones into economic hotspots and accelerating the socio-spatial shifts behind the urbanisation - and rising land values - of Senegal’s border areas.

Conclusion

In the 21st century, the world has become essentially urban. Urbanisation, which reached its peak in the developed countries, is now occurring rapidly and anarchically in the countries of the Global South. Senegal, like other West African countries, is experiencing accelerated urbanisation, which is increasingly taking place in rural areas. This process is underpinned by several factors.

The crises in the rural world, which have led to a search for alternative livelihoods, have been accompanied by a major socio-spatial transformation or recomposition. The development of new sectors of activity fuelled by cross-border dynamics and town/country relations has had a dazzling impact on border villages. This is reflected in rapid spatial sprawl resulting from both intrinsic demographic dynamism and migratory influxes from inland villages and towns. Proximity to the secondary towns, ease of travel, the border effect and land accessibility are the driving forces behind the urbanisation process. As a result, while this urbanisation has raised the standard of living of rural dwellers, it can also be fertile ground for the development of phenomena such as food insecurity, lack of access to land and problems in planning and sanitation.

The views and analyses expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung.

Ayimpam, S. 2020. Mobilités, circulations et frontières. Migrations, mobilités et développement en Afrique [Mobilities, circulations and borders. Migrations, mobility and development in Africa]. Anthropologie & développement, 51.
Bennafla, K. 1999. La fin des territoires nationaux? État et commerce transfrontalier en Afrique centrale [The end of national territories? State and border trade in Central Africa]. Politique Africaine, 1(73), 1–26.
Bennafla, K. 2012. Pour une géographie des bordures à l'heure globale: frontières et espaces d'activités 'informelles [Toward a geography of borderlands in the global age: borders and spaces of ‘informal’ activity]. Géographie, Université Paris Ouest Nanterre La Défense.
Fall, A.S. et Guèye, C. (dir). 2005. Urbain-Rural, l'hybridation en marche [Urban-Rural: Hybridization in progress]. Dakar: Enda Tiers Monde.
Lacroix, T. 2018. Transnationales: espace, temps, politique [Transnationalism: Space, Time, Politics]. Geography. University of Paris East.

Cas des frontières Sénégal-Gambie et Sénégal-Guinée [Borders, actor strategies and territorialities in Senegambia. Case of the Senegal-Gambia and Senegal-Guinea Conakry borders]. PhD thesis in geography and planning, Université Paul Valéry Montpellier.

  • 3

items.title: From Fields to Frontiers: The Unplanned Urban Rise of Rural Senegal Commentary As Senegal's rural borderlands transform under urbanisation, villages emerge as frontiers of change. Fueled by trade, migration, and identity ties. They reveal how urban growth is reshaping life along the Senegal-Gambia border and redefining rural space. Abdou Kadry Mané, Ibrahima Diombaty
